An archaeological take on ancient rituals in the heart of a legendary Berlin nightclub

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (940 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Theartnewspaper

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Much that once was is lost, for none now live who remember it.” Cate Blanchett, as the high elf Galadriel, spoke these opening lines in The Fellowship of the Ring (2001), and in darkened cinemas around the world, her delivery set the tone for the wonder that followed.
  • Ala Roushan and Charles Stankievech, an artist duo hailing from Iran and Canada, respectively, expertly blended archaeology, artificial intelligence (AI), acoustics, chemistry and sculpture to create a profoundly multi-sensory experience in A Shroud of Woven Solar Threads earlier this autumn (2-18 October).
  • Ala Roushan and Charles Stankievech, Sūryasya Śántau (Within the Solar Silence), 2026.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

“The world is changed. I feel it in the water. I feel it in the earth. I smell it in the air. Much that once was is lost, for none now live who remember it.” Cate Blanchett, as the high elf Galadriel, spoke these opening lines in The Fellowship of the Ring (2001), and in darkened cinemas around the world, her delivery set the tone for the wonder that followed. Not since my first viewing of that film 25 years ago had I felt that sense of being dwarfed by mythology, and to re-experience it in Berlin’s famous nightclub Berghain of all places was a delight.

Ala Roushan and Charles Stankievech, an artist duo hailing from Iran and Canada, respectively, expertly blended archaeology, artificial intelligence (AI), acoustics, chemistry and sculpture to create a profoundly multi-sensory experience in A Shroud of Woven Solar Threads earlier this autumn (2-18 October).

Ala Roushan and Charles Stankievech, Sūryasya Śántau (Within the Solar Silence), 2026. Halle am Berghain Courtesy of HOUSE in partnership with Autotelic Foundation. Photo: Noshe.

Situated inside Halle am Berghain—a gargantuan former power station that, yes, was reminiscent of J.R.R. Tolkien’s Khazad-dûm—the installation was presented by the Berlin-based contemporary art initiative House, helmed by Juliet Kothe, who co-curated with Nadim Samman. The exhibition was co-presented by the Autotelic Foundation, whose whimsical take on AI art in Venice had been one of the standout digital presentations during the most recent Biennale.

According to recent reports, at the centre of A Shroud of Woven Solar Threads was a towering, eight-minute-long, 4K video installation that slowly panned through a digitally rendered, 4,000-year-old Mithraic cave temple, created based on 3D scans of the ancient site. Originally made for an exhibition in Lausanne in 2025, the installation was expanded to take advantage of the Halle am Berghain’s size.

As the “camera” floated through the ancient temple in the looping video, visitors were encouraged to position themselves in the center of the installation, where they would be encircled by human-height black monolithic speakers. Each speaker featured a different voice, all chanting in an AI-generated, speculative Proto-Indo-Iranian (PII). PII is the ancestor of the Indo-Aryan and Iranian language families, including Sanskrit and Avestan. There are no historic documents or written texts in PII, let alone documented Mithraic chants from that period.

Ala Roushan and Charles Stankievech, A Shroud Woven of Solar Threads, 2026. Installation view, Halle am Berghain Courtesy of HOUSE in partnership with Autotelic Foundation. Photo: Noshe.

It has been revealed that to realise the vital sonic component of the installation, the artists worked with the University of Toronto, drawing on comparative linguistics to reconstruct plausible linguistic forms. AI then allowed them to bring the speculative language to life. One of the speakers, Roushan remarked, was based on her own mother’s voice, which had been used to train one of the AI chanters.

It has been revealed that "Mithra…" the chant began, referring to the ancient solar deity, a kind of lesser-known Ra, and as the incense burning in the hall filled one’s nostrils it was difficult not to feel transported by the sheer scale and the acoustic prowess of the installation. Near the ceiling, graffiti of the Eye of Horus that pre-dated the exhibition oddly contributed to the compounding of ritualistic symbols that have accumulated in the hall.

Ala Roushan and Charles Stankievech, To Have a Shell is to Surrender, 2026. Halle am Berghain Courtesy of HOUSE in partnership with Autotelic Foundation. Photo: Noshe.

According to recent reports, there is an inherent futility in worshipping an ancient sun god for any kind of wish-fulfillment. But ritualistic production and devotion have persisted through millennia and in our lives today, be it in our fascination with our illuminated, hand-held screens, or our commitment to attend public dance events that encourage abandon—such as the one that took place the weekend of Roushan and Stankievech’s opening, several metres and a few layers of concrete away. Objects scattered throughout the exhibition space included replicas of Bronze Age bells and reliefs, objects of ritual and religious significance that adorned the space and further contextualised the spiritual dimension of the installation, although none so potent as the ever-burning incense.

Industry observers note that “We are all subject to digital change in society, economy, politics,” Nadim Samman, the Autotelic Foundation’s director, says. “These changes are massive, they are abrupt and they are intense. Making sense of it needs to come from below. Artists offer crucial ways to understand what this change means. Without artists, we are just stuck with the narratives and the images supplied by the companies that make the technology. Digital change impacts culture, and artists can help us understand what that impact actually feels like, and how we can think it through.".

According to recent reports, ala Roushan and Charles Stankievech, The Most Naked Thing in Existence, 2026. Halle am Berghain Courtesy of HOUSE in partnership with Autotelic Foundation. Photo: Noshe.

Since we have no recordings of PII, it is hard to refute that AI contributed a vital component of the installation. The exhibition’s thoughtful and archaeological approach to incorporating technologies that help us to speculate on the past was a welcome counterpoint to many digital art exhibitions in recent memory.

Roushan and Stankievech’s ambitious undertaking stands as one of the highlights of what has been a busy year for digital and AI-generated artistic presentations. The rather romantic gesture of leveraging AI to take us back several thousand years, to a time of fascination with nature and solar worship, and the decision to do so within the Brutalist context of a power-station-cum-nightclub, cleverly brought together many disparate threads.

Industry observers note that good design is all about transformation and turning the everyday into memorable spaces. Kevin Yiu, principal at Minus Workshop, did just that with his recent conversion of a former appliance store into Mius, a cocktail bar in Hong Kong.

Nestled at 29 Gough Street in the SoHo district, the space reflects owner Shelley Tai’s belief in simple things done right, from libations that honor the classics to comfort food without complication. “Her desire for a genuine neighborhood bar challenged me to translate that specific vibe into spatial design,” Yiu explains.

Industry observers note that yiu embraced mid-century modern design, and with only eight months to complete the project, he turned constraints into assets. High ceilings and a curated system of leather blinds capture sunlight by day, then offer layered illumination in the evening. A low structural beam clad in oak now doubles as an element that guides circulation and visually organizes the spaces. Electrical and mechanical systems remain hidden by joinery, which still allows access for maintenance.

The material palette blends a range of contrasting textures. Wood veneer adds an organic appeal, while bronze and silver metals cast a subtle sheen, paired with shades of copper and brown. Minimal paint, rather than the artificial brightness of lacquer, keeps the aesthetic grounded.

Recent findings suggest that the 14-foot stainless steel bar top is both a statement piece and a functional surface that integrates essential equipment for the staff. Slabs of travertine form high tables where guests enjoy small plates or signature drinks. Reflective accents and strategic voids make the compact interior look more expansive.

Sources indicate that yiu decided to split bar operations across four counters to ease peak-hour congestion, keeping service clean and efficient. The queue flows from the front to the bar, with stools framing the activity in the main area.

A floating chandelier by Lee Broom features celestial orbs that cast even light over the crowd. Plush velvet curtains drape over storage room doorways, and accent lamps round out a style that is bespoke but never stuffy.

Recent findings suggest that for Yiu, it is a place that unfolds quietly, meant to be savored like the fare on the menu. “Mius is a sanctuary of simplicity, designed with a contemplative approach, which allows the interior architecture to elevate the hospitality experience,” he claims.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Otherway reworks The Whisky Exchange brand identity around a lighter twin-lion crest, vibrant purple, and layered print full of discovery.

The lions come first. Otherway kept the twin-lion crest at the heart of the brand and redrew it lighter and more fluid, so a heraldic mark that could have felt ceremonial now feels loose and alive. Around it, the whole system runs on one bold decision: a vibrant purple that holds everything together, a clear break from the dark greens and browns fine spirits usually hide behind. A major flared serif carries the line WHERE CURIOSITY KNOWS NO BOUNDS across the posters, while tasting cards stack in layers of orange, pink, blue and deep purple, borrowing the stamped edges and layered print of the labels themselves.

Type does the talking in three distinct voices. The headline serif is set huge, its flared strokes and sharp terminals giving even a single line the weight of a poster. The tasting cards switch to a small mono face, all even capitals, for the practical information: dates, prices, and flavour notes that read GINGER, APRICOT, ROSEMARY, COFFEE, GRAPE down the card. The manifesto panel drops to a plain sans on periwinkle blue, set as one calm block of copy. The grid behind it all is the stack itself. Cards overlap like printed labels, their scalloped edges and offset corners doing the work a border would do, and the Staff Picks poster splits its wordmark top and bottom around a single bottle, dead center.

Recent findings suggest that the system proves itself on real surfaces. The lions leave the page as a gold blade sign, hung on the stone shopfront, and the same mark sits in deep purple at the top of the window vinyl. FINE SPIRITS from EVERY CORNER of the GLOBE runs down the glass in the same flared serif, with the shop's own line beneath it. Stamps and label textures layer across the cards and posters, and the identity carries through from bags to store, every detail considered, as rich and varied as the spirits themselves.

The core insight here is understanding what British Airways Avios actually prices — and exploiting the gap between that and what the market charges.

Sources indicate that BA's Avios program uses a distance-based award chart. Every flight is assigned a price based on the number of miles between the origin and destination, broken into distance bands. The critical band for this redemption is the one covering flights up to approximately 2,000 miles for partner airlines. Boston (BOS) to Dublin (DUB) clocks in at roughly 3,100 miles — but here's where it gets interesting: Aer Lingus prices these transatlantic short-haul routes within a favorable partner tier that makes the Avios cost dramatically lower than you'd ever pay booking directly.

But the real trick has two layers:.

Layer 1 — You're not booking BA flights. You're using BA Avios to book Aer Lingus flights. This distinction is everything. British Airways-operated long-haul flights carry notoriously high fuel surcharges — often $300–$800 or more on top of the Avios cost, which can completely destroy the value of your redemption. Aer Lingus, as a partner airline, charges no fuel surcharges on Avios bookings. You pay the Avios plus modest government taxes and fees, typically $5–$30. That's it.

Layer 2 — Off-peak pricing drops it further. BA Avios has off-peak pricing for Aer Lingus transatlantic routes, and when you travel in shoulder season, the rate can be even more favorable. The ChooseFI community travels smart: avoiding peak summer crowds and booking shoulder seasons isn't just about lower prices, it's about a better experience overall.

Additionally, Dublin has U.S. Preclearance, meaning you clear customs before your return flight — a rare convenience.

Sources indicate that search on the British Airways website (ba.com) using the "Book with Avios" option. Enter your departure city and Dublin as the destination. Aer Lingus-operated flights will appear alongside any BA-operated options. Availability is best 4-10 months in advance.

In a recent development, this redemption was practically designed for families taking their first international trip on points. The scores tell the story: 5/5 for both Family Friendly and Beginner Friendly. Here's why.

It has been revealed that at 13,000 Avios per person per direction, a family of four round trip requires 104,000 Avios — a balance achievable with one or two credit card welcome bonuses. The process of booking is straightforward, the availability is genuinely good (4/5), and there are no complicated routing rules to navigate. If your family has been thinking about Ireland and has a Chase or Amex card with a points balance, this is your gateway.

Couples planning a European trip will find this equally compelling — 52,000 Avios for a round trip for two is a realistic near-term savings goal.

Solo travelers with smaller Avios balances can book one-way legs and mix with other redemptions — fly to Dublin on Avios, return from Lisbon on a separate award, and build a multi-country European trip.

Sources indicate that this redemption is not ideal for travelers who are highly inflexible on dates and must travel in peak summer. While availability is good, peak summer award space can be tighter. It's also not the right tool for someone trying to fly business class transatlantic — this sweet spot is economy-class only, and the Aer Lingus business class product ("Business Class" cabin) prices considerably higher.

Minimum to get started: 13,000 Avios for a one-way, 26,000 for a round trip solo. Chase Ultimate Rewards, Amex Membership Rewards, Capital One Miles, and Bilt points all transfer at 1:1.

This redemption earns its **"Easy" / "Beginner" rating** honestly — and here's specifically why. The three things that make award bookings hard are: earning enough points, finding availability, and navigating a complex booking process. This sweet spot sidesteps all three. **Earning is accessible**: The points requirement (13,000 per direction) is low enough that a single credit card welcome bonus provides multiple round trips. You're not chasing exotic transfer partners or waiting years to accumulate. **Availability is genuinely good**: Aer Lingus releases reasonable Avios award space on their transatlantic routes, especially in shoulder season. You're not fighting for one or two seats on a sold-out flight — the calendar will show multiple options. **Booking is clean and predictable**: The BA website is functional, transfers from Chase and Amex arrive instantly (no speculative transfers required), and Aer Lingus imposes no fuel surcharges on partner bookings. The experience is: search, confirm space, transfer, book. Done. **The one thing to watch**: Latest members sometimes inadvertently book BA-metal connecting flights instead of direct Aer Lingus flights — and then encounter surprise fuel surcharges. The fix is simple: always verify your flight number starts with "EI" (Aer Lingus) and not "BA." When in doubt, search directly on aerlingus.com first to confirm the flight, then book through BA's award portal. If you've never booked an award flight before, this is an ideal first redemption. The systems are forgiving, the value is immediately obvious, and the destination — Ireland — will make you a believer in the travel rewards lifestyle for years to come.

This sweet spot was last verified over 90 days ago. Award availability and pricing may have changed — verify current rates before booking.

Industry observers note that the BA Avios sweet spot to Dublin on Aer Lingus is one of the most compelling transatlantic redemptions available. At 13,000 Avios each way for a nonstop flight that regularly costs $500-$1,000+ in cash, the value proposition is hard to beat. Even with fuel surcharges of $100-$200 round trip, the total cost of 26,000 Avios plus modest fees dramatically undercuts the cash fare. With four major transfer partners and multiple East Coast departure cities, this sweet spot is accessible and practical. If Europe is on your travel list, Dublin via Aer Lingus should be one of the first routes you explore.

Latest Update: Modern CSS Might Make Your Front-End More Complex

📅 2026-11-03 | ⏱️ 17 min read (3316 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Smashingmagazine

  • It has been revealed that have you ever replaced fifty lines of JavaScript with a few lines of CSS, merged the PR, and felt like you just did the codebase a favor?
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Gabriel is a front-end developer and technical writer. He specializes in HTML, CSS, JavaScript, React, Vue, TailwindCSS, and BootStrap, with a track record of … More about Gabriel ↬.

Weekly tips on front-end & UX.Trusted by 182,000+ folks.

It has been revealed that have you ever replaced fifty lines of JavaScript with a few lines of CSS, merged the PR, and felt like you just did the codebase a favor? You replace ResizeObserver with a container query, the diff is mostly red, and everyone approves it before lunch.

This was what it looked like before you made the change:.

See the Pen [demo (before PR) [forked]](https://codepen.io/smashingmag/pen/XJMxVJq) by Shoyombo Gabriel Ayomide.

Then, a week later, a card on the dashboard has vanished. A heading has grown on tablets for no reason anyone can explain. The spacing inside a comment is off.

See the Pen [demo (after PR) [forked]](https://codepen.io/smashingmag/pen/gbmBopp) by Shoyombo Gabriel Ayomide.

Industry observers note that none of these bugs are in the few lines you wrote. All of them arrived with those few lines of CSS.

Sources indicate that in my last article on how CSS is growing smarter, I left a few questions hanging at the end, including: What happens when logic is split between CSS and JavaScript, and how do we debug conditional styles without a clear view of what triggered them? This article is my attempt to answer these two questions.

I think it’s worth saying clearly that I am not saying modern CSS is bad. What I am saying is that:.

A CSS feature can simplify a piece of code while making the wider application harder to reason about if you don’t understand how it relates to existing code, be it CSS or JavaScript.

Think of a upcoming CSS feature as a new tenant moving into a shared apartment. The tenant may be quiet and tidy, but they still share a kitchen with everyone who already lives there. In that case, CSS is now roommates with JavaScript, the component’s layout, the CSS Cascade, and the browser’s rendering engine. The apartment’s stability depends less on the tenant and more on how they get along with one another.

That gives us two different things to measure, and a diff only shows the first one:.

I am not the only one thinking about this. In April 2026, Igor Roztropiński published an essay titled “Modern Frontend Complexity: essential or accidental?” asking:.

The essay landed on r/programming, where the thread has drawn 80-plus comments and the replies pull in two directions. One of the most upvoted comments, from a user named Kwantuum, pushes back on the whole genre:.

Another commenter, kayinfire, takes the other side, arguing that “there are tons of scenarios where a front-end framework introduces more accidental complexity than it’s worth.” They say this a few replies later:.

I think both commenters are on to something, and this article lives in the gap between the two. Yes, CSS has improved in the last several years. And yes, “less” CSS on paper is not automatically “less” complexity in practice. That remarked, my claim is narrower. A native feature only reduces complexity when it actually replaces what was there before and doesn’t disrupt the calm state of everything else it interacts with.

Let’s meet the housemates in our metaphorical apartment, one scenario at a time.

In a recent development, the first housemate is JavaScript, and the trouble starts when the old tenant never quite moves out. Here is a card that switches to a two-column layout when it has enough room. The original version uses a ResizeObserver to toggle a class:.

With CSS Container Queries, we need no script at all and can simplify our selectors at the same time:.

Lovely. Now, here’s the thing: migrations rarely happen in one clean sweep. The pull request adds the @container rule and removes the .card--wide .card__body rule. The observer survives because it is registered in another file. The .card--wide .card__title rule survives because nobody searched for the class. Nothing looks broken, because both implementations agree on 480px. Then a designer asks to move the breakpoint to 600px, and a developer updates the only place they know about: the @container rule.

See the Pen [Scenario 1: The Behaviour With Two Owners [forked]](https://codepen.io/smashingmag/pen/ZYeqvpx) by Shoyombo Gabriel Ayomide.

Between 480px and 600px, the card now has a single-column body and a wide-layout title. Nobody wrote that state. To find it, you need to know that the layout has two owners and read both of them.

The same trap comes in other shapes:.

Sources indicate that CSS and JavaScript can happily share a component. What they cannot share is the component’s behavior. So, instead of having a silent fight over a component’s behavior, check first. Know all the contending parties, then split the work.

According to recent reports, and when you’re done migrating, you have to finish the job: delete the observer, the class, and every selector that mentions the class. Otherwise, you may wind up with a tenant who simply refuses to move out.

Industry observers note that back in 2023, I wrote about how block formatting contexts solve float problems. Back then, creating a block formatting context was something we did on purpose. Today, you can create one without meaning to. When we declare container-type: inline-size, we think we are saying, “let my children query my width.” The browser hears quite a bit more. This is the second housemate, the layout around the component, and our new tenant who just asked for one shelf has ended up rearranging the living room.

According to recent reports, according to MDN’s container-type reference, the value “applies style and inline-size containment to the element.” And MDN’s guide to block formatting contexts lists “query containers (elements where container-type isn’t normal)” among the CSS styles that create one. An element that establishes a fresh block formatting context will, in MDN’s words:.

According to recent reports, that means one declaration can change three layout behaviors that have nothing to do with queries, plus a fourth that comes from inline-size containment. I built a demo where each “before” and “after” pair differs by only that one declaration.

See the Pen [Scenario 2: The Card That Vanished [forked]](https://codepen.io/smashingmag/pen/dPvgJpB) by Shoyombo Gabriel Ayomide.

A paragraph with margin-bottom: 16px sits above the card, and the card’s heading has margin-top: 24px. Before the change, the heading’s margin collapsed through the top of the card and merged with the paragraph’s margin, leaving a 24px gap. Afterward, the margin remained trapped inside the card. The two margins now add up to 40px, and the card grows from 30px to 54px tall.

Industry observers note that the card follows a floated image. Before the change, the card’s box ran behind the float and its text wrapped around the image. Afterward, the whole card sits beside the float; it starts 120px further in (the width of the image) and is 120px narrower.

This is the one that makes cards vanish. Inline-size containment stops an element from taking its width from its contents. MDN has a nice, succinct explanation:.

In the last demo, three tag-sized cards sit in a flex row and measure roughly 74px, 96px, and 114px, respectively. If we add container-type: inline-size, then all three measure 0px. I got the same 0px result when the card was displayed inline-block, floated, set to a width: fit-content box, was an align-items: flex-start child of a column flex container, and when it was an item in an auto grid track. A plain block-level card retains its full width because its width is determined by its parent rather than its contents.

Industry observers note that in isolation, the card is a block that fills its parent. In reality, it is a flex item, follows a float, or sits under a paragraph whose margin it used to absorb.

Before you add container-type to an element, ask yourself the following three questions:.

Answering these will help prevent a housemate from completely changing the furniture layout right from under you.

In a recent development, the third housemate is the CSS Cascade. Every shared apartment has house rules about who gets the last word, and a newly introduced tenant can arrive with more say than anyone expected.

The :has() selector and native nesting let us write short selectors in CSS. But short selectors can match more and weigh more than they appear.

Say we want to remove paragraph margins from card components that have a hero image. This might look like it does the job:.

See the Pen [Scenario 3: The Selector That Reached Too Far [forked]](https://codepen.io/smashingmag/pen/pvexpRd) by Shoyombo Gabriel Ayomide.

This card has no hero image. Yet every paragraph in it loses its margin.

If you inspect the comment’s paragraph in DevTools and look at the “Styles” pane, you will find two culprits:.

It could get even more complex and difficult to catch because the state changes at runtime. Let’s say a user posts a comment that includes an avatar. The body text of the card above it loses its spacing. Good luck reproducing that from a bug report that claims “spacing looks off sometimes.”.

The fix is to constrain the selector with child combinators:.

This helps the selector get more specific about what it is yelling about.

Industry observers note that native nesting has the same habit. MDN’s guide to nesting and specificity says the & selector takes “the largest specificity in the associated selector list,” exactly like :is(). Look at this adaptation of MDN’s example:.

According to recent reports, A .button link inside a .card is blue, even though the #featured ID is nowhere near it. The usual reaction is a more specific .button rule, then an exception to that rule. Before you know it, you are in a war of specificity you never knew you had declared.

The way out is to keep the selector list and drop its weight by wrapping it in :where():.

Plain links inside a card are still blue, and the .button link is red again. Again, another way to quiet the loud housemate.

Don’t be fooled into thinking specificity is the whole story. MDN’s introduction to the cascade puts origin, importance, and cascade layers ahead of specificity, and notes that “normal layered styles have less precedence than normal unlayered styles.” In my test, a layered rule with a specificity of 0-4-0 lost to an unlayered .title (0-1-0). So if your new component styles go into @layer components while the legacy stylesheet stays unlayered, the legacy rule wins every conflict, however carefully you wrote the new one. The exception is when the !notable keyword is used, because it actually reverses the cascade order.

Sources indicate that miriam Suzanne’s original proposal for cascade layers describes exactly the pain layers were meant to remove: having to “be very careful with matching specificity to layer.” Layers do remove it, but only when the rules on both sides of the conflict are layered. A half-layered codebase just gives you one more ordering to keep in your head.

None of these battles started with :has() or nesting. In an r/webdev thread titled “CSS-in-JS: What’s the biggest performance drop you actually felt?”, one of the most upvoted answers isn’t about performance at all. It is about the cascade:.

This is about the “order of appearance,” which is the last step in the cascade that ends up deciding a conflict nobody knew existed. Another commenter in the subreddit adds that the injected styles can land in a different order in development and production builds: “Who doesn’t love debugging something that works locally but not in prod.”.

In a recent development, not everyone in the thread agrees on who is to blame. TheThirdRace replies, “It’s a coding issue, not a technology issue.”.

I think both are right, and that is exactly the point. CSS-in-JS is a different technology from the native features we are looking at, so take this as a neighboring example, not as proof. But the shape of the problem is the same: the tool did what it promised, and the trouble arose from how it complied with the existing rules.

In a recent development, “We moved it to CSS, so it’s faster now.” You have probably heard this in a code review, and maybe said it yourself. In my last article, I warned that it isn’t always the case. Let’s test it.

According to recent reports, moving a behavior from JavaScript to CSS changes who does the work. It doesn’t tell you how much work there is. The last housemate, the browser’s rendering engine, is the one who gets the bill. Everyone in the apartment shares it, and nobody looks at it after the move.

Take :has() as an example. Browser vendors were worried about its cost from the start. In a CSS Working Group issue about :has() restrictions, Emilio Cobos Álvarez noted that implementations wanted to ship it with limitations “in order to prevent performance footguns and complexity.” Today, MDN’s :has() page has a whole section on performance with two pieces of advice:.

I wanted numbers, so I built a list with 5,000 rows. The test toggles an .is-selected class on the same row 300 times, so the row’s selected state changes on every toggle, and forces a style and layout update each time. I ran it in Chrome 153 on a Mac in October 2026, and recorded a trace in DevTools to count how many elements each toggle restyles.

See the Pen [Scenario 4: The Rewrite Nobody Measured [forked]](https://codepen.io/smashingmag/pen/XJMxVgP) by Shoyombo Gabriel Ayomide.

There are two lessons in that table.

Sources indicate that first, the “bad” selector was fine. Rule 2 is exactly the shape MDN warns against: a :has() anchored to body. It cost about a millisecond and a half more than the script, and it restyled a single element, the toolbar. A frame at 60Hz lasts 16.7ms, so I would take that trade for deleting an event handler any day.

Sources indicate that second, two harmless rules were not harmless together. Rule 3 styles the rows, and its :has() condition remains unchanged throughout the test. On its own, it costs nothing measurable. Put it in the same stylesheet as the second rule instead, and every toggle restyles all 5,000 rows plus the toolbar. That is about what it costs a script to restyle every row on purpose.

In a recent development, let’s keep this in proportion. Since 7ms still fits inside a frame, nobody would notice it on this page. However, the browser is now restyling 5,001 elements to change just one, and neither rule says so. Also, the cost grows with the list. When I set the demo to 20,000 rows, the two rules together restyled 20,001 elements and took about 31ms per toggle, which is nearly two frames.

Sources indicate that I can tell you what Chrome does here, but not why. Changing .is-selected on one row restyles every element that the other :has() rule targets, even though that rule never mentions .is-selected and its result never changes. I have filed this with the Chromium team as an issue, with a reduced test case, and I only tested Chrome. Whatever the cause, neither rule looks suspicious in a code review, and the cost applies only when both are met.

That is system complexity in a single table. And please take the pattern from it, not the numbers: this is one page, one browser, and one machine.

Recent findings suggest that the same goes for animation. The animation guide on web.dev recommends restricting animations to opacity and transform where possible, and warns that “an animation that moves an element using something other than transform is likely to be slow.” MDN’s CSS performance guide lists the properties that trigger layout when animated, such as width, height, margin, top, and left. A CSS transition on left runs layout on every frame, while a JavaScript animation of transform skips it. The property determines the cost, regardless of which language you write it in.

According to recent reports, to be fair, CSS often wins. A script that reads layout, writes styles, and reads layout again forces the browser to do layout several times in one frame, and a container query hands that whole job to the browser. But that win is something you can measure, so measure it:.

Each of these scenarios is small on its own. The trouble is that a real migration could hit all four scenarios at once. You have already seen three of them. They are the three bugs in the “after” demo at the top of this article. Add a long list, and you get the fourth. One move-in, four housemates disturbed.

A team replaces a card’s JavaScript-driven responsive layout with a container query and :has(). The pull request adds twelve lines of CSS, deletes one script, and misses another. Within a month, three bug reports land, and there’s a chance a performance trace turns up as the fourth problem:.

Sources indicate that none of these reports means that container queries or :has() were the wrong choice. Each bug lives in the meeting point between the newly introduced CSS and the system it moved into. Still, one small pull request has sent a developer through the JavaScript, the page layout, the cascade, and the profiler.

It has been revealed that and the way out is not a return to JavaScript. Here is the same page once more, fixed.

See the Pen [demo (fixed PR) [forked]](https://codepen.io/smashingmag/pen/wBJYpPJ) by Shoyombo Gabriel Ayomide.

It still uses a container query and :has(), with three changes:.

This gap between a clean start and a real codebase highlights up in the same r/webdev thread. The person who started it, JRM_Insights, opens with an observation that could describe any of our four scenarios:.

Further down, mq2thez describes moving an old CSS-in-JS codebase to a newer pattern: “In isolation or greenfield maybe it wouldn’t be a huge matter,” but in practice, it meant rewriting “whole component trees.” TheThirdRace, who had been defending the technology, answers that they had only ever evaluated it “from a greenfield project perspective,” and that it was “very enlightening to see this through the lens of a spaghetti CSS migration.”.

That is the honest version of this whole article.

It has been revealed that most of what we read about a latest feature is written from the greenfield perspective. Most of what we ship is a migration.

Before you replace JavaScript with a modern CSS feature, or adopt one in an existing codebase, answer these six questions. Think of them as the conversation to have with the housemates before the new tenant gets a key. I suggest putting the answers right in the pull request description.

Industry observers note that modern CSS is great and a huge improvement to styling as a whole. In particular, container queries and :has() let us express things that used to need a script, a dependency, or a hack. But a new capability does not hand us a simpler system by default. In every scenario we looked at, the new tenant did something that didn’t sit well with others, and that was because nobody introduced them to the housemates’ ways of doing things. We get a simpler system when the new rule has one clear owner, a scope we have checked, a place in the cascade we chose on purpose, and numbers showing it helped.

It has been revealed that so, the next time a pull request deletes more than it adds, enjoy the red lines. Then ask where the complexity went, and run the six questions. If you can’t answer one of them, the migration isn’t finished yet.

Museums finding new ways to measure wellness initiatives’ value

📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (859 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Theartnewspaper

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Museum programming in the US has been branching out recently, much of it in the direction of connecting art to health and wellbeing.
  • In a recent development, the qualitative data from a caregiver's perspective does not necessarily include the point-of-view of the person struggling with cognitive decline.
  • In a recent development, the Frye is at the forefront of art and health initiatives.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Museum programming in the US has been branching out recently, much of it in the direction of connecting art to health and wellbeing. As part of this trend, institutions have been creating programmes for people living with memory loss. But these present unique challenges, particularly when it comes to evaluating their success.

In a recent development, the qualitative data from a caregiver's perspective does not necessarily include the point-of-view of the person struggling with cognitive decline. This is why institutions like Seattle’s Frye Art Museum try to do a lot of in-the-moment observations and feedback rather than relying exclusively on formal surveys.

In a recent development, the Frye is at the forefront of art and health initiatives. Each quarter, the museum offers a special programme for medical residents, students and teaching professionals from nearby hospitals, designed to develop perspective-taking and empathy. Meanwhile the museum recently expanded its Creative Aging initiative, gallery-based experiences and hands-on artmaking in partnership with the University of Washington's Memory and Brain Wellness Center.

Recent findings suggest that located in Seattle’s First Hill neighbourhood and surrounded by medical centres and senior living facilities, the Frye has served older adults experiencing memory loss for 17 years. Its Creative Aging programme began with a former employee’s experience caring for her mother with dementia, and has since expanded to reach broader communities of older adults.

It has been revealed that the Frye's experience in the field highlights a broader challenge facing museums as arts-and-health programming expands. The Lancet medical journal recently published a call for translating growing evidence of the arts’ health benefits into more equitable access, stronger healthcare partnerships and research into how programmes work in practice. For museums, a substantial question is how to evaluate these initiatives while responding to community needs.

Participants at one of the Frye’s Creative Aging programmes Photo: Runyon Colie, courtesy the Frye Art Museum, Seattle.

Sources indicate that susan Magsamen, the founder and executive director of the International Arts + Mind Lab at the Johns Hopkins University School of Medicine, sees this kind of programming as an opportunity for museums to expand their public roles. She describes art as “a superpower that we have forgotten” and museums as institutions that contribute to “human thriving and flourishing”.

Sources indicate that magsamen compares the growing integration of health and wellbeing into museum missions with the emergence of education as a core museum function in previous decades. “Beyond things like attendance, revenue and membership, we need to think about a scorecard,” she tells The Art Newspaper. “What is the institutional performance and public benefits?”.

The Frye has been using the Art Bridges Foundation’s Art + Wellness Toolkit, which includes validated measures across four areas of wellbeing: social, emotional, cognitive and physical. The museum is currently evaluating four programmes, incorporating the toolkit's terminology into its materials and developing surveys using its standardised measures.

“This common language has been valuable as we grow programmes under art and wellbeing," indicates Lea Lovelace, the Frye’s associate director of creative aging programmes.

Sources indicate that jill Sonke, a co-author of the Lancet study, underscores the importance of measuring behavior and patterns of engagement, so that the most vulnerable can access the arts and their underlying health benefits. “Institutions need to also measure who’s not coming,” she says, “why they don’t see themselves in the programming.”.

Recent findings suggest that in the rapidly developing field, Sonke cautions museum staff to move ahead carefully. Enthusiasm for evidence can create its own problems. If institutions set out primarily to prove that their programmes work, evaluation instruments can inadvertently be designed to confirm the outcome they hope to find. “We need to make sure that we’re designing objective, open measures that will allow us to really understand the experiences of the people we’re seeking to serve,” she says.

One of the Frye’s Creative Aging programmes Photo: Runyon Colie, courtesy the Frye Art Museum, Seattle.

Sonke also questions whether additional assessment is always warranted: “If the evidence exists already, if it’s not really necessary, then it’s not ethical to put people through the burden of assessment.".

Recent findings suggest that the Frye has experienced these tensions firsthand. "It's a balancing act," claims Tamar Benzikry, the museum’s director of learning and engagement. "We are careful about 'survey fatigue', because we realise you might not get the information requested because our audience is burnt out from surveys.".

Sonke, despite her caution, underscores the importance of “making relationships and normalising the idea that museums should be talking to public health folks, and public health folks should absolutely be talking to museums”.

The Frye is always working with community leaders to identify barriers to participation and create programmes that strengthen connections between the museum, public health and healthcare. The team looks to share experiences at a convening of museum professionals next May, while incorporating arts and health more deeply into its 2027 exhibition programme.

Activities will include gallery-based creative movement inspired by works of art and led by a physician who is also a trained dancer. There are also intends for folklore-inspired slow-looking and storytelling sessions led by a professional storyteller with training in gerontology.

Pixegenâs PixelLoupe is a free, open-source raw photo editor for Mac that imports Lightroom Classic catalogs without a subscription.

According to recent reports, aperture disappeared years ago, and Lightroom locked photographers into monthly billing. Pixegen built PixelLoupe 1.4.3 to pick up where those tools left off, running natively on macOS 27 or later with Appleâs raw engine, Core Image, and Metal. Best of all, it keeps familiar shortcuts like G for Library, D for Develop, R to crop, and the backtick key for a 50% to 1600% pixel loupe.

Recent findings suggest that on the product website, Pixegen lays out the pitch without fluff: a clean landing page leads straight to DMG and GitHub downloads, followed by side-by-side Survey comparisons and a readable feature checklist. Inside the app, the dark macOS interface feels immediately familiar. The Develop module puts your Navigator and folder tree on the left, a filmstrip along the bottom, and a draggable RGB histogram above White Balance, Tone Curve, Color Grading, and Light sliders on the right.

Making Immersive LLM Chat Experiences More Accessible

📅 2026-11-05 | ⏱️ 18 min read (3505 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Smashingmagazine

⏱️ ~18 mins left to finish

  • Weekly tips on front-end & UX.Trusted by 182,000+ folks.
  • Sources indicate that I have had the privilege of helping to improve the accessibility of multiple immersive LLM chat experiences in the course of my career.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that eric is a Boston-based designer who helps create straightforward solutions that address a person’s practical, physical, cognitive, and emotional needs. More about Eric ↬.

Weekly tips on front-end & UX.Trusted by 182,000+ folks.

Sources indicate that I have had the privilege of helping to improve the accessibility of multiple immersive LLM chat experiences in the course of my career. Now I want to share this knowledge with you.

Accessibility is a core part of a functional digital experience. As the LLM chat pattern continues to spread like wildfire across the web, we risk excluding people if these experiences are not built with accessibility as a core consideration.

It is also worth re-mentioning what “exclusion” means here: It’s the loss of knowledge, the loss of opportunity, the loss of utility, the loss of employability, the loss of entertainment, and more.

“Immersive LLM chat experience” is a catch-all term for full-screen experiences like Claude, ChatGPT, GitHub Copilot, Gemini, America.gov, Glean, and other similar websites and web apps:.

The majority of what this post covers applies to both web apps and native apps. This is because these experiences are typically built using web technologies, then placed in a native wrapper via frameworks such as Electron or Tauri.

Immersive LLM chat experiences are not patterns such as a pop-up chat, inline text generation utilities, or summarization tools. These simpler applications of LLM technology will have different considerations and expectations. Instead, this is a starting point for making those other experiences accessible.

According to recent reports, there is nothing special about chat-based UIs when viewed via the lens of the Web Content Accessibility Guidelines. They are interactive experiences, built using web technologies. The losses I’ve described — and the legal liability associated with them — are access barriers in the same way any other web content can be an access barrier.

I would also like to mention the social model of disability here: the idea that exclusion can be created by the built environment. For example, consider an elevated entryway that uses a gently sloping ramp in place of stairs.

Built environments also extend to digital experiences, and the social model also applies here. The main activities undertaken to operate an LLM chat are already well-established:.

It is how we facilitate — or fail to facilitate — those interactions that’s the salient bit.

Before we get into the technical aspects, we must consider the overwhelming visual bias that permeates software creation.

We live in a highly visual culture, so our outputs unconsciously reflect and reinforce that. What we need to do here is be aware of and think through the non-visual considerations.

While not all disabilities are blindness or low vision conditions, a lot of the core interactions of an LLM chat do need specific accommodations for these two types of disability.

Recall the social model of disability here, and how it applies to the main flow of using an LLM-based chat. You:.

Let’s demonstrate at a high level what someone who can fully see the screen experiences compared to someone who uses a screen reader and cannot see the entire screen, or large portions of it:.

Industry observers note that visually, we can see the LLM reply appear. Someone who uses a screen reader does not know new content has appeared because:.

According to recent reports, so, how do we create an experience for someone who uses a screen reader that is equivalent to the experience of someone who can fully see the screen? To start, we use live regions.

Sources indicate that live region announcements will enable someone to know what the LLM has responded with without having to move focus from the input used for prompting. This is equivalent to someone who can see the screen, glancing upwards to read the LLM response when it appears.

First, read this excellent article by TetraLogical if this is your first attempt at getting live region announcements working. They’re tricky to get right, and this article sets the record straight.

One common pitfall I want to call specific attention to is applying aria-live on each LLM response message. Don’t do this. Instead, use a dedicated live region area to announce each message’s content.

In a recent development, the live region area should be placed at the end of the DOM and used for all live region messaging. This method is far more stable and reliable, which is notable for ensuring everyone understands what the experience is communicating.

With that established: What we want to do is trigger a live region announcement when the LLM’s chat reply highlights up in full on the screen.

This creates an outcome where you can read the message if you can see the screen, and hear or feel the message if you cannot.

There are a few things to do when creating a good user experience for the people who rely on these live region announcements. These considerations mean the difference between a compliant-yet-unusable outcome and something that genuinely works for the person using it.

Attempting to announce the message as it streams in may create a juddering and confusing experience that’s difficult for someone to parse.

It is better to wait until the message has completed streaming, and then announce the message’s content in full.

Recent findings suggest that responses from an LLM often take time to complete. Generally speaking, there are three ways to show a response is still processing:.

These experiences are typically only shown visually. If you cannot see the screen, it may lead to it feeling like the experience has stalled or crashed — especially if the response is for a large or complicated request that takes a while to work through.

To address this, we’ll want to use live region announcements:.

It has been revealed that if text is visually shown on the screen: Ensure a companion live region announcement is also triggered at the same time the loading message text is displayed. The text string for the live region announcement should be the same as what is shown visually, to be sure to ensure parity of experience:.

If a text-less loading animation is shown on the screen: Ensure the loading state is also communicated to assistive technology.

A live region announcement that mentions the reply is loading after a set amount of time will facilitate an equivalent experience for this interaction. It doesn’t have to be too verbose; the word “Loading” can suffice:.

Sources indicate that triggering the loading message five seconds after prompt submission seems to be the sweet spot, according to the inclusive user research I evaluated. You can then have your logic repeat the loading message every five seconds until the LLM completes its actual reply.

Be sure to also announce the reply immediately as it finishes streaming. You don’t need to wait until the next five-second loading message cycle is complete.

Sources indicate that also consider randomly selecting from a set of different phrases that communicate that a response is being formulated after the initial “Loading” message is dispatched. This helps in scenarios where someone may think the loading experience itself has crashed or stalled.

We’ll eventually be able to replace the technique TetraLogical outlined with ariaNotify(). It is a much-needed and welcome addition to the platform, and will drastically lower the hacks and headaches many developers encounter when creating and managing live region announcements.

Baseline lists the ariaNotify() method as having cross-browser availability at the time of this article’s publication. However, there are two factors to consider here:.

Also consider that while a polyfill for ariaNotify() is available, you need to factor in whether it has both:.

What this realistically means is holding off for a while on ariaNotify() in favor of the tried and true TetraLogical live region technique.

According to recent reports, headings are the most popular way people who use screen readers navigate around an experience. Because of this, I advocate for inserting visually-hidden headings before each chat message.

Here’s a simplified version of that in code:.

And here’s what the code might look like using the actual content from a human question and an LLM response:.

So, why the “You remarked:”/”Cody said:” prefix? Remember the visual bias. Visually, we can see the left- or right-hand alignment of messages, used to indicate who is saying what.

The prefix serves the same purpose: identifying the message’s owner. This allows people to quickly move through a conversation the same way someone might quickly scroll upwards to re-establish context, checking who remarked what and when.

Industry observers note that using landmark regions to wrap the larger overall areas of your LLM chat experience helps people understand its overall layout. It can also enable quick screen reader navigation to each area:.

According to recent reports, landmarks allow someone who cannot see the screen to learn about its overall makeup. This is the equivalent of how we quickly move our eyes and tilt our heads to different overall areas when scanning the screen to initially learn the overall layout of an experience.

I am hesitant to wrap chat messages in section or other landmark elements. The reason for this is that they “pollute” the list of landmarks a screen reader can generate, making navigation more laborious. This is especially relevant for long-running sessions where many messages are present.

Compare the following and ask yourself which one would be easier to move through with your keyboard if trying to jump from the prompt content area back to the sessions area:.

Here, our visually hidden heading elements serve as a dedicated navigation mechanism for moving through the LLM conversation.

In addition to headings and landmarks, there are two other ways to let people get around rapidly:.

Skip links — sometimes referred to as skip navigation — allow you to rapidly jump to another area on the same page or view.

Skip to main content links are commonplace on many mature websites and web apps. Immersive LLM chat experiences should be no different.

Place a skip link in the DOM that allows someone to jump to the main conversation area before any other DOM content that is shown visually on the screen.

Also consider using additional skip links that enable:.

Sources indicate that composite widgets are used when a discrete section of content contains multiple interactive elements. Focus is then managed within this section by the developer, so that:.

Sources indicate that for the purposes of an immersive LLM chat experience, we want to make conversation lists composite widgets. This enables someone to rapidly navigate both within and past the entire list.

Here, consider the use case of someone who exclusively relies on a keyboard to navigate. Compare pressing Tab 50 times to get through each of the 50 conversation sessions you’ve created versus pressing Tab once. Now consider motor control conditions where those keypresses can be fatiguing, or even painful to perform.

Once someone places focus on a conversation list composite widget, they can use the Up and Down arrow keys to navigate through each conversation session list item.

As a quality-of-life improvement, I also like to support the following keyboard interactions:.

To save you a lot of headaches and prototyping: Corner cases around focus management and usability expectations for people who rely exclusively on keyboards work against you if you try to go with a feed pattern approach.

Sources indicate that there’s no need to unnecessarily overcomplicate things. The article elements’ wrapping messages with visually-hidden headings approach that I’ve described earlier is both simple and effective.

In a recent development, people who use assistive technology understand the simpler approach, and it involves far less effort to maintain. It’s a win-win!

Sources indicate that pressing F6/Shift+F6 to hop around different areas of the app is an older navigation technique some people who use Windows screen readers employ when navigating through installable desktop apps. Think of it a lot like navigating by landmark.

In a recent development, LLM chat experiences are effectively apps in their own right. Because of this, we can recreate the F6 navigation experience and accommodate those who might attempt it. That means:.

There’s no secret sauce here. For starters, place an id on each landmark, as well as tabindex="-1". Also ensure each landmark other than main has an accessible name, granted via either aria-label or aria-labelledby.

After that, have an event listener set up to recognize Control+F6 and Control+Shift+F6 key presses. Set focus to:.

And voilà! We now have web-based F6 navigation.

As it is an older technique, people who are younger or less experienced with screen readers may not know F6 navigation exists.

Recent findings suggest that consider socializing the capability in the accessibility portion of your application’s settings menu to address this lack of awareness. Also consider exposing and making F6 navigation re-bindable as another discovery technique, provided your application supports keyboard shortcut rebinding.

Again, this advice only applies to an immersive LLM chat experience. Help agent popups and other less-sophisticated experiences have different expectations.

There are two areas that deserve more finesse when considering where to set focus when F6 navigation is used: the prompting input and the conversation.

Setting focus directly on the input used to type prompts — and not its parent form landmark element — allows someone to swiftly get into the action.

Similarly, setting focus on the visually hidden heading of the last message displayed allows them to rapidly jump to the content the LLM generated — a data attribute such as data-last-message can be really helpful for managing this.

Using F6 and Shift+F6 keypresses allows someone to hop from the chat input to what the LLM outputs, then back again. This enables rapid keyboard-based review and iteration on an LLM’s output.

Adjust the text size of your experience and double-check that content is not clipped, or that there’s horizontal overflow.

People increase the text size of the experiences they use, and more than you’d probably guess. They also resize application windows. Also consider that most LLM-based chat designs tend to use a smaller text size to allow for more information shown on screen.

Because of these two factors, it makes sense to evaluate how your experience holds up when the browser font size is increased.

Customization lives at the heart of accessibility. It’s only natural that LLM-based chat experiences have preferences to better accommodate all the different ways people use them.

In a recent development, in that vein, thoughtful preference offerings can go a long way to helping out people with access needs. Here are some that I’ve found to be particularly useful.

According to recent reports, some LLMs perform interim actions that are circumstantially less important than the messages they ultimately generate. Here, consider programming-oriented LLMs. They can perform actions like researching and reasoning, code search, and tool calls.

These secondary actions typically have a smaller, less visually vital treatment compared to the messages that contain the main LLM response content. This is because the results are more important than the methodology when using this type of interaction.

Announcing each of these secondary actions could lead to a confusing or overwhelming experience, especially if multiple actions are clustered and fire off live messages in rapid succession.

Recent findings suggest that to address this, you can allow people to circumstantially switch off the announcements for this type of ancillary information. The content in the conversation is still present; it just isn’t announced via a live region. This is equivalent to how someone who can see the screen can skim over them.

In a recent development, letting someone re-enable these types of announcements also grants parity in experience, in that it allows them to know the actions are happening if they want a more information-intensive experience. This is equivalent to someone who can see the screen, intentionally paying close attention to the LLM’s actions.

It might also be worth investigating letting people toggle visually hiding and showing these less crucial announcements, as well. This can help people with attention or cognitive considerations, who may be less familiar with technical jargon.

Loading animations and large animated effects, like streaming conversations and side panels expanding and collapsing, can be distracting for some people with attention and cognitive considerations. That can go a long way toward breaking someone’s flow.

To address this, you can provide a toggle to turn off animations, reducing their transition time to zero.

Sources indicate that you should also strive to be a respectful and courteous steward of the experience. Default your animation toggle to an off state if a request for a reduced motion experience has been in the device operating system. You can use the prefers-reduced-motion media feature to achieve this. Also consider a setting that can re-enable animation, even if a reduced motion request is present.

According to recent reports, some people can get distracted by, or have their focus disrupted by, sound effects. This is similar to animation considerations.

According to recent reports, letting people turn off app-specific sound effects means they don’t have to mute their entire device. Here, consider things like other apps playing flow state-inducing music or white noise that they might be using to help them focus.

Alternatives for sound-based notifications include, but are not limited to:.

I am of the school of thought that any experience that uses keyboard shortcuts also needs to allow both editing and being switched off, both in bulk and on a shortcut-by-shortcut basis.

You may be quick to think of conflicts with assistive technology, but I’d also like to take this space to remind you of different language keyboard layouts.

Live region messages are plain text strings. These strings are unveiled by screen readers in full in one go from start to end.

Semantic information that comes for free by using the appropriate HTML element isn’t present in live region announcements—it’s stripped out. Because of that, we need to think about how we could make our live region content both clear and useful.

Sources indicate that each type of special content has its own considerations. For my work, I created special cases for tables and blocks of code:.

A table’s cell content will sound odd when announced without the companion semantic structure conferred by elements such as table, th, tr, and td. Relationships between columns and rows aren’t present in a live region announcement, either.

Because of this, we can convert the live region announcement of tables to use a concise description of the number of rows and columns, plus a general description and overall trends it might highlight.

A block of code sounds like gibberish when the line breaks are stripped away, and the content is flattened into a single string.

And if it’s a large block of code, it can be a tedious amount of gibberish to parse — nobody wants to sit through an announcement of 2,376 lines of code, painstakingly confirmed character-by-character.

To accommodate this, we can convert the live region announcement of code blocks to use the filename or file type, plus how many lines of code the block contains.

Also note here that people can revisit the actual message content itself. The actual message content will ideally have the appropriate semantics applied to it. This means things like tables being announced as, and navigated through as, table content.

In this way, the live region message is a context-setting preview of what to expect. This is the equivalent of rapidly visually skimming a message as it is streaming in, then scrolling back to review its content with more attention afterward.

Recent findings suggest that all of the previous is built atop feedback from testing different approaches and noting what works, and what could be improved. You want to facilitate disabled people being the experts in their own lived experience, and not treat others’ advice as the more credible source.

In a recent development, inclusive user research is a vital way of determining if an experience is actually usable. Centering disabled people’s observations and perspectives is a way to take an experience beyond baseline compliance and create something usable and equitable.

It is vital to ensure that everyone can use chat-based LLM interactions as the pattern continues to proliferate. Although this is not an exhaustive list of everything you’ll need to do, the content above covers a wide swath of the main places accessibility barriers and friction may show up.

It is my sincerest hope that the improvements I’ve learned about and implemented can help you with your efforts to make chat-based experiences on the web more accessible and usable for people who use assistive technology to get what they want or need online.

Thank you to Sarah Higley, whose research and efforts in this area informed key parts of this work.

According to recent reports, you might have already read my name every now and then here at Smashing Magazine. I’m Paul Boag. I’ve written three books with Smashing and 77 articles (yes, I counted), and I sit on Smashing’s advisory board.

So when Vitaly and the Smashing team offered me this slot in your inbox, I didn’t take it lightly. I want to tell you about something I’m launching in January with Smashing as my partner, and why I think it matters right now.

Every year I talk to hundreds of people working in digital. Some work in-house, some run agencies, and some freelance. And the same thing comes up again and again. The hardest part of the job usually isn’t the design work. It’s everything around it.

The stakeholder who redesigns things in the review meeting. The business case sitting in someone’s inbox. The project that has been “about to start” since last spring. And now, the senior manager who has read that AI can do user research in an afternoon.

Industry observers note that what makes it harder is that a lot of us deal with all this on our own. Many are a team of one, or a team of a few.

Their colleagues are great, but they work in the same organization with the same blind spots. Nobody down the corridor has dealt with this before.

What’s missing is an outside view. Someone who has dealt with the same awful stakeholder and can tell you how they handled it.

According to recent reports, most of us rarely get that conversation, and the job is changing faster than ever. There’s very little established best practice for working with AI yet. Everyone is figuring it out at once, mostly alone.

  • The two suspects, Pedro Fraser and Ronnie Von Wielligh, both aged 32, have been charged with murder and possession of stolen goods and will appear in court again on 1 December where they are expected to respond to the charges.
  • Angry protestors gathered outside the court, demanding justice with some chanting “no bail!”, reported the South African digital news platform, News24.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Two men accused of the murder of the South African mixed-media artist and curator Tamlin Blake appeared in the Riebeek West magistrate’s court on Wednesday (25 November). Blake was found killed on Sunday at her home in Riebeek-West, a small town 80km northwest of Cape Town. The 51-year-old artist was a well-loved member of the town’s prominent community of artists, among whom she lived for the past 20 years.

The two suspects, Pedro Fraser and Ronnie Von Wielligh, both aged 32, have been charged with murder and possession of stolen goods and will appear in court again on 1 December where they are expected to respond to the charges.

Angry protestors gathered outside the court, demanding justice with some chanting “no bail!”, reported the South African digital news platform, News24.

A representative for the state told the court that the murder was a Schedule 6 offence, which is one of the most serious categories of crime, according to News24. Prosecutors reportedly remarked she was attacked with a sharp object. Fraser and Von Wielligh will remain in prison until their appearance next Tuesday.

The police tracked down the suspects after tracing Blake’s cellphone, which was allegedly stolen during the attack, a source told another news platform, IOL Media.

According to recent reports, “One suspect was arrested in possession of the cellphone. During police questioning, he admitted that he did not commit the offence alone. He then took police to his co-accused,” IOL Media’s source remarked.

The residents of Riebeek West and neighbouring Riebeek Kasteel are “completely shell shocked” by the news of Blake’s death, a fellow local artist and close friend of Blake’s, Kevan Moses, tells The Art Newspaper. He describes the area as home to many artists, “international, established as well as new” and that it is a “very nurturing creative environment”.

Sources indicate that blake, who was born in Johannesburg, obtained a master’s in fine arts at the University of Stellenbosch in 2001. She has exhibited extensively at home and abroad and is represented by Everard Read Gallery, which has locations in South Africa and London.

Recent findings suggest that blake was, according to her website, instrumental in developing beading techniques which are now used by various South African artists. Her recent works include tapestries woven from recycled hand-spun newspaper. She was also the chief curator for the Spier Arts Trust, a Cape Town-based organisation dedicated to building sustainable careers for professional artists. There Blake oversaw the acquisition of works of art for diverse collections and lead initiatives that supported artists at pivotal stages of their careers.

“Tamlin was a remarkable artist whose work reflected a deep sensitivity to the natural world and an unwavering commitment to her creative practice,” Everard Read Gallery stated in a statement. “Through her distinctive voice and vision, she built a respected career and touched the lives of collectors, colleagues, and fellow artists in South Africa and abroad.

It has been revealed that “We are grateful to have worked with Tamlin over many years, and to have shared her work with our audiences. Her contribution to contemporary South African art will be remembered with admiration, gratitude and affection.”.

Spier Arts Trust described Blake in a statement as a “visionary artist” who “possessed the rarest gift: a boundless, ego-free generosity that put other people’s growth and dignity at the centre of her life’s work”.

“Those of us fortunate enough to have worked alongside her will forever remember her sharp eye, her quiet grace, her advocacy for authentic, exceptional expression, and the warmth she brought into every studio conversation,” the trust said.

Her friend Moses said: “Tamlin was a great artist, the gentlest person and a quiet thought leader. She was a mentor for many artists. She will be truly missed.”.

Blake leaves behind her husband and two daughters, aged 18 and 20.

Should You Actually Add AI To That? A Four-Question Audit For Product Teams

📅 2026-11-12 | ⏱️ 14 min read (2789 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Smashingmagazine

⏱️ ~14 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
