  • Weekly tips on front-end & UX.Trusted by 182,000+ folks.
  • A product team at a large health insurer wants to add AI that writes the full written determination for benefits appeals specialists.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Victor Yocco, PhD, is a UX Researcher with a focus on AI and the author of Designing Agentic AI Experiences (CRC Press, 2026), Design for the Mind (Manning, … More about Victor ↬.

Weekly tips on front-end & UX.Trusted by 182,000+ folks.

A product team at a large health insurer wants to add AI that writes the full written determination for benefits appeals specialists. The technology works as specified. However, the specialists stop using it, and the ones who keep using it take longer on each case than the ones who ignore it.

Industry observers note that A short evaluation with the specialists surfaces the problem fast: reading an AI-written determination carefully enough to sign it takes about as long as writing one, and the specialist also has to check for mistakes they would never have made themselves. The feature adds work to a task these people had already mastered.

It has been revealed that rescoping the release fixes it. A second version surfaces the policy provisions and prior decisions relevant to each appeal and leaves the writing to the specialist. The search step disappears, review time drops, and the part of the job the specialist is good at stays where it was.

The technology is identical in both versions, and the difference is which part of the task the AI handles.

Recent findings suggest that every interface change costs the user something before it pays anything back. They have to rebuild their picture of how the tool works, learn where things are now, and decide how far to trust what the AI hands them. Nelson Cowan’s review of working memory research (2001) put the limit at about four items held in mind at once. All three of those jobs draw on the same small supply.

It has been revealed that an AI feature in an enterprise software setting requires more from the user than a redesigned menu, because it changes what they do all day. Hand the synthesis to an AI and the user becomes a checker. Give it the recommendation too, and the job shrinks to signing off. Either change costs user attention, and for people whose training is their standing at work, either one can feel like a demotion. For example, in one study, Sophia Ackerhans (2025) and colleagues found that physicians asked to sign AI-assisted decisions reported a more serious threat to their professional identity, and explanations of the AI’s reasoning raised both trust and that threat together.

We can call that the break-even line. Returns to people come in three forms:.

According to recent reports, for example, an AI-powered fraud screening tool indicates the errors-caught form at work, since the analyst reviews flags they would never have raised themselves, which costs attention, and the catch rate pays for it. That puts the feature above the break-even line.

According to recent reports, four questions can help your team locate the break-even line before design work starts. Each one produces a design condition the brief can act on.

These questions do not replace the build decision. Funding, strategy, and existing commitments all weigh on that, and four questions cannot see any of it.

Run through all four questions together, since no single question settles the matter alone. Do it while the feature is still a proposal, before anyone sinks weeks into design. You will also need at least one person who does the task for a living, such as a loan officer, analyst, or benefits specialist. They do not have to sit in the roadmap meeting, and a short conversation tells you where the mental effort actually sits and whether the feature would help or add work.

Count everything the task asks of the user: the thinking, the clicking, and the checking they will owe once AI is involved. Fewer clicks proves nothing on its own, because a feature can cut clicks and still leave the person working harder. Write down the cost even when it goes up, since Question 2 may find a return that pays for it.

A loan officer reading 40 financial disclosures to find the three that conflict with lending policy is thinking hard, and AI that surfaces those conflicts cuts that demand directly. Compare that with typing a loan number into a tracking system, which costs a few seconds and almost no thought. Pre-filling that field relocates the cost instead of removing it, because the officer now checks what the machine entered. Conventional wisdom indicates to automate the repetitive and monotonous tasks, and the pre-filled field is where that advice misfires. In this example:.

You can find the tasks worth automating by comparing total effort before and after. Count the checking the user inherits on the after side.

Who the user is matters as much as what the task is. One feature can clear the line for a junior analyst and fall short for a senior one. Hand a junior analyst an AI-drafted risk summary, and they gain a starting point they lack the pattern library to produce on their own. A senior analyst, however, reads that same summary against the analysis already formed in their head, spends four minutes doing it, and learns nothing.

Industry observers note that A finding like that tells you who to ship to. Scope the addition to the group it serves.

Sources indicate that compare the AI approach against the user’s current method, including the spreadsheets and workarounds they built for themselves. Genuine ambiguity is one reason AI comes out ahead when someone explores options, produces a starting point, or looks for patterns too numerous to spot by hand. Scale, speed, and consistency across a group of people doing the same job are three more. A fourth is catching what the current method reliably misses, which is how the fraud screening tool earns its place. The advantage disappears once the user has a practiced route to a known answer.

For example, an HR team building a succession planning tool finds the answer running both ways inside one product. Using AI to surface internal candidates whose skill combinations nobody would think to search for wins on ambiguity and scale together, since no single right answer exists and manual review of that search space would take weeks. Drafting the notification email after someone picks a candidate loses to the method already in place. The format is familiar, the writing takes two minutes, and the person sending it holds firm opinions about tone. The candidate search earns the addition. The email draft layers an interaction onto a task that runs fine without one.

In a recent development, the nature of the input and the shape of the output are separate decisions. A task can hold genuine ambiguity and still call for a structured visual result instead of a conversational one. Pair this audit with a modality evaluation for the output side.

Recent findings suggest that every AI system makes mistakes. The question is whether your user will notice. Start with how visible the error is. Then weigh what it costs when nobody catches it, and whether the user still has the skill to catch it. Question 1 asks what checking costs. This one asks whether checking is even possible.

Error visibility varies enormously, and product teams tend to estimate it badly. For example, an AI trip planner that suggests a museum on the day it closes produces an invisible error, because nothing in the output looks wrong. The traveler finds out while standing outside a locked door in Tokyo. Compare that with a suggested flight that departs before the connecting flight lands, where the contradiction sits right there on the screen.

Automation bias makes the invisible cases worse. Raja Parasuraman and Dietrich Manzey (2010) reviewed decades of human factors research showing that people defer to automated output even when that output is wrong, across aviation, medicine, and process control. Trust climbs fast, and rarely as a conscious decision. Once it does, users stop applying the scrutiny that would catch the mistake.

Map the error surface, meaning the ways this feature can be wrong, before design work starts. List the three likeliest error types. Rate each one on visibility to the user and consequence if it slips through. Any combination of low visibility and high consequence becomes a design requirement.

In a recent development, show owners where the output came from and how the system produced it. That is provenance, and it is what lets trust settle at the right level. People who can see the source, the data behind it, and when it was pulled catch errors more often. Tell the traveler that a restaurant’s hours came from a page cached in March and they know what to check. A confident-sounding paragraph with no source attached leaves them guessing.

Letting the routine work go is a real benefit of adding AI. Nobody needs to protect a specialist’s ability to format a citation or an analyst’s ability to total a column by hand, and arguing to preserve skills the technology has absorbed wastes everyone’s time.

According to recent reports, still, the judgment that catches the machine’s mistakes stays exempt from replacement. That judgment makes every other delegation safe, and disuse degrades it like any other skill.

Research in radiology indicates how fast a suggestion can override a reader’s own judgment. In a 2023 experiment, Thomas Dratsch and colleagues had 27 radiologists read mammograms alongside what they were told was an AI system (a simulation created solely for the experiment). The radiologists worked through a 10-image training set where the suggested category was always correct, then 40 more mammograms with incorrect suggestions planted in 12 of them. The result indicated how incorrect AI suggestions damaged diagnostic accuracy at every experience level. The most experienced readers, averaging 15 years, assigned the correct category 82.3% of the time when the suggestion was right and 45.5% of the time when it was wrong, while the least experienced group fell from 79.7% to 19.8%. Experience softened the effect without preventing it. A year of deferring to the same system, with the judgment it replaced sitting unused, leaves a reader in a weaker position than the one these radiologists started from.

Sources indicate that question 3 looks at your user today. Extend the same test 12 months forward and you arrive at Question 4. Teams that answer the first and skip the second read the resulting failures as a quality problem in the model, when the cause is the human judgment they took out of daily use.

In a recent development, ask whether this user could judge the quality of the output 12 months from now if the feature vanished tomorrow. When the answer is no, the design needs a mechanism that keeps verification skill in use. Periodic blind review works well and costs little, with the user forming a judgment before seeing what the AI produced. Rotating a share of cases off AI assistance does a similar job, as does a weekly comparison between machine output and a human-produced version.

Table 1 below gathers the four questions, the signals pointing each way, and the condition each one produces.

In a recent development, table 1: The AI Addition Decision Matrix. Clear answers across all four questions point toward building the feature as proposed. A poor answer on Question 1 calls for a design condition or a change in scope, unless Question 2 finds a return that covers the cost. Questions 2 and 4 work the same way without that exception. A poor answer on Question 3 can stop the build.

Put the conditions in the design brief, where they become project requirements. Teams reduce AI features to yes or no because roadmap reviews demand it, and that throws away everything the audit found. A feature that answers well on Questions 1 and 2 and poorly on Question 3 proceeds only with provenance built in. Write that in on day one. Requirements that arrive at the end read as polish, and teams cut polish when timelines slip.

According to recent reports, let’s return to the insurer scenario from our opening. The first version of the tool fails Question 1. Writing a determination takes sustained thought, and the AI that produces the draft moves that effort into verification without reducing the total. An hour with the four questions would surface that before the first version reaches design.

Sources indicate that question 2 points in the same direction. Appeals determinations follow a familiar structure, and specialists reach the answer through a practiced route. The ambiguity in the task sits earlier, in finding which provisions and prior decisions apply.

It has been revealed that question 3 raises the stakes. A wrong determination affects someone’s medical coverage, and an error buried in fluent prose stays invisible until the next appeal arrives. That answer produces the provenance requirement in the second version, which cites the source document and retrieval date for every provision it surfaces.

Industry observers note that question 4 explains why the second version holds up. Specialists still write every determination, so the judgment that evaluates the retrieved material stays in daily use. Keeping version one would train specialists for a year to approve text they no longer have the practice to assess.

AI-generated meeting summaries sit inside products that millions of people open every day, and the audit reaches a different answer for them.

On Question 1, a summary removes the work of writing notes and adds the work of checking whether it attributed a decision to the right person. Total effort drops for the participant who never took notes. For the person who always took the notes and circulated them, the trade is closer, and the verification lands on them. That split is exactly what Question 1 is built to surface.

It has been revealed that question 2 compares the summary against someone typing while half-listening, which produces patchy notes. A summary beats that on completeness and on consistency from meeting to meeting, so the feature clears this question for most teams.

Industry observers note that A summary that assigns a commitment to the wrong person looks exactly like a correct one, and nobody rereads the transcript to check. On Question 3, low visibility and real consequence together turn into a requirement for a linked source timestamp behind every action item.

It has been revealed that the feature clears Question 4, and the design needs no mechanism. Nobody loses a skill worth protecting by giving up meeting notes, and the participants keep making every decision the summary records.

According to recent reports, two clear answers, one segment finding, and one condition. The timestamps ship with the feature, and the habitual note-taker is the segment the team checks after launch.

You can run this before the next AI feature reaches your roadmap.

Everett Rogers (2003) called this pro-innovation bias, the assumption that upcoming capability means progress before anyone verifies the benefit, and competitive pressure turns a rival’s announcement into an internal mandate. An hour of structured questions gives your team a way to answer that pressure.

According to recent reports, audit results land badly when a designer presents them as reasons the feature should not exist. The conditions are the useful output, so bring those into the product review.

Start by naming the segment the feature serves, which makes the answer a yes for someone. Hand over the error surface as a requirement with a cost attached. A product manager can act on a request for timestamps behind every attributed decision, and nobody can act on a worry that users might not trust the output. Then offer the change in scope without waiting to be asked. A version that surfaces the provisions instead of writing the determination is a smaller build with a better adoption story, and that framing moves a roadmap conversation forward.

A sentence that works out loud: We think this clears the bar for junior analysts and adds a verification step for senior analysts, so we would scope it to onboarding and revisit the rest next quarter.

Recent findings suggest that the attention a person can spend in a working day stays fixed no matter how good your model gets. Before the next feature reaches design, write down what it will cost the person doing the work and which of the three returns pays for it. With both answers in hand, your team can walk into the roadmap review with a scope to propose.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

DixonBaxi sets the EA SPORTS FC 27 brand identity free, turning one triangle into dozens of forms built to move, remix and belong to fans.

The triangle was already the mark. FC spent three years building something millions love, and DixonBaxi kept the shape at the centre of it rather than redrawing it. The studio set it loose instead. One triangle now arrives as a wireframe outline, a dotted halftone field, a pixelated edge, a solid green slab or a beam of light, and the identity holds together because the shape never changes, only the way it behaves. The line on the posters states it plainly: FC is not played, it is lived.

It has been revealed that type does the loud work. The grid sheet sets EVERYONE'S PLAYING in stacked condensed caps, with the FC27 lockup held to two columns and the tagline stretched across five, and the annotations name the voice: Cruyff Sans Condensed Medium for the calls to action, Cruyff Sans Regular for the small print. THE WORLD'S GAME runs the same way on the billboards, the heavy word GAME dropped below a tracked-out THE WORLD'S in the same condensed face.

The grid behind it all is the triangle itself. Lines flow across the posters the way crowds move, and the lockups sit inside the same diagonal geometry, so a headline, a phone screen and a stadium banner all read as one system. The palette stays close to the pitch: electric green leads, with hot pink, purple and blue in support, and black fields that let the colour shout.

The system proves itself on real objects. A green controller carries the triangle pattern across its shell, with the FC27 lockup set into the touchpad in pale gold. The Grounds, the open world where players meet, compete and chat beyond the pitch, gets its own mark: FC set inside a heavy triangle, with SCREEN, STADIUM and STREET as its three corners, and ten small variants beneath it in pink, purple, green and white.

Industry observers note that the launch trailer pulled 5+ million views on day one, and the same triangles now run from campaign posters to the game itself, built for a community the studio counts at one billion fans. Make it your Club, your City, your Crew, your Home, your Block: the identity hands the shape to the fans and lets them finish it.

AI Sped Up The Build: How Can Accessibility Testing Keep Up?

📅 2026-11-17 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1089 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Smashingmagazine

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that andrew Chung is Chief Product Officer at Level Access, a Leader in the first Gartner® Magic Quadrant™ for Digital Accessibility Platforms.
  • Weekly tips on front-end & UX.Trusted by 182,000+ folks.
  • This article has been kindly supported by our dear friends at Level Access, who help organizations create accessible and legally compliant websites, mobile apps, software, and other digital experiences.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that andrew Chung is Chief Product Officer at Level Access, a Leader in the first Gartner® Magic Quadrant™ for Digital Accessibility Platforms. Andrew leads the … More about Andrew ↬.

Weekly tips on front-end & UX.Trusted by 182,000+ folks.

This article has been kindly supported by our dear friends at Level Access, who help organizations create accessible and legally compliant websites, mobile apps, software, and other digital experiences. Thank you!

In a recent development, lately, I’ve been thinking and writing a lot about what AI is doing to product development, and what that means for accessibility. The thing that has my wheels turning is a finding from Level Access’s 2026 State of Digital Accessibility Report. Basically: AI is helping us hit fast-forward on the build, but testing practices haven’t kept up.

We asked more than 2,500 professionals where they noticed AI was speeding up their work in the SDLC. Most mentioned they noticed gains in planning (58%), design (61%), and development (51%). But QA and testing lagged behind: Only 30% said AI had sped up that stage.

These results point to a two-speed workflow. AI has turbocharged design, planning, and development, while checking and validation are still running at a very different pace. This means a lot of teams are likely racing through the build, then being forced to hit the brakes the moment someone has to answer a pretty fundamental question: Is this thing actually accessible?

Accessibility has historically been treated as a QA bottleneck, and AI is pushing far more work into it, faster. If your team has already shifted left on accessibility, you’re off to a good start. But AI has reshuffled the workflow, so even proactive teams need to work out where those early checks belong now.

Recent findings suggest that this matters because right now, the web is moving in the wrong direction. WebAIM’s latest scan of the top million home pages found that automatically detected errors per home page rose 10.1% in a year, from 51 to 56.1 per page. WebAIM cited AI-assisted coding as one possible contributing factor.

So how do we get validation out of first gear? How do we build human judgment into the workflow as AI keeps pushing the pace?

We looked at the organizations that are improving across every accessibility metric they track (a group we call the “improvers”) to find out what they’re doing differently.

According to recent reports, here’s what stood out: AI adoption made the smallest difference of anything we measured. Improvers use AI at a similar rate to everyone else we surveyed. Their edge highlights up in the maturity of their surrounding accessibility practices — things like training, communication, and a culture of accessibility.

A quick caveat: This is survey data, so it only shows correlation, and mature programs may simply be better at tracking and reporting their wins. Even so, this finding was hard to ignore.

And it got even more interesting. Professionals in mature accessibility programs were nearly six times as likely to say AI helps them prioritize challenges. They were also nearly three times as likely to say it helps them tackle accessibility more proactively in development.

It has been revealed that in other words, AI works best as an amplifier of a strong program. With context, testing, environments, and guardrails in place, agents can take on a large share of the work from drafting through to operations, and much of the time lost to waiting and handoffs goes away. People stay responsible for deciding what to build and for approving what ships.

So let me ask you: When it comes to accessibility, where does human judgment sit in your workflow today?

Industry observers note that not sure? Here’s a quick way to find out.

In a recent development, pick a feature you shipped recently and trace it from the first Figma frame to production. Mark every moment a person decided whether it would work for someone using a keyboard, a screen reader, or their browser at 400% zoom.

Recent findings suggest that how many marks did you get? If most of them cluster at the end of creation, you’re likely heading to one of two places: You’ll either ship accessibility barriers or spend the time you saved upstream fixing them later, when they’re harder and costlier to fix.

Here’s how to avoid both outcomes by building the right accessibility checks and judgment calls into the work your team is already doing.

As AI takes on more work, people need to stay involved at three points: finding concerns, fixing them, and documenting the evidence. Each one plugs into a step your team already takes, like a handoff, a pull request, or a review, so nothing new gets added to the timeline, and accessibility keeps pace with the work that’s in motion.

Context fades fast. Put the first judgment checkpoints as close to the creation work as you can:.

Found the issue? Great. Fix it while it’s fresh. When issues end up as tickets, make sure the context travels with them. They should carry the element, the repro, the related WCAG criterion, a suggested fix, and the PR link, so context doesn’t leak.

The worst time to start gathering evidence is when somebody’s asking for it.

It has been revealed that every check, fix, and judgment call throughout the process described above should ideally leave a trail. A fix isn’t done until something fails if the issue comes back. Ask your AI assistant to write the regression test with the fix and put the finding link and any judgment call in the PR description. That’s the receipt.

A passing test shows a known matter hasn’t returned. It doesn’t show the experience works. For what automation can’t cover, add a short note to the PR: what you tested, with which assistive technology, and any judgment calls you made.

AI has given digital creation a speed boost, but broadly speaking, validating the work hasn’t kept pace. Closing that gap isn’t about adopting more AI in more places or abandoning the toolset that helped make your team faster.

According to our data, the opportunity in front of teams is to build the practice around that toolset, so that human judgment is flagged, embedded, and acted on earlier, and more often.

We’ve only scratched the surface of what our data tells us about AI and accessibility. If you’re curious about what else we found, check out the 2026 State of Digital Accessibility Report. There’s plenty more to unpack.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Lisa Marei Schmidt has been appointed as the new director of two major museums in Bern: Kunstmuseum Bern and Zentrum Paul Klee. The board of trustees of the foundation that oversees both institutions selected Schmidt from 97 applicants following an international search, according to a release. She will lead on artistic direction and also chair the museums' management board.

According to recent reports, schmidt has directed the Brücke-Museum in Berlin, home to the world’s largest collection of works by artists from the German Expressionist group Die Brücke, since 2017. During that time she has co-curated exhibitions exploring complex and sometimes dark aspects of the history of German Expressionism, such as Escape into Art? The Brücke Painters in the Nazi Period (2019) and Whose Expression? The Brücke Artists and Colonialism (2021–22). Under her direction, the museum has also strengthened its work in provenance research, restoration, art education and digitisation. The German Association of Art Critics (AICA) named the Brücke-Museum as its museum of the year for 2023.

Born in 1978, Schmidt studied art history in Marburg, Amsterdam and Berlin, and curating contemporary art at the Royal College of Art in London. Before joining the Brücke-Museum, she worked as a research trainee at Kunstsammlung Nordrhein-Westfalen and served as a curator at Berlin's Hamburger Bahnhof from 2012 to 2017. In 2020, she curated Bonzo's Dream by Swiss artist Vivian Suter, which received AICA's Special Exhibition award.

In a recent development, “To me, museums are places where art and people meet,” Schmidt mentioned in a statement. "They provide space for encounters, new perspectives and dialogue across society." She said she looked forward to getting to know the teams in Bern and building on the distinctive qualities of the two museums, which have shared strategic leadership under the umbrella foundation Kunstmuseum Bern – Zentrum Paul Klee since 2015.

Schmidt will also inherit a pressing challenge at Kunstmuseum Bern. In June, voters in the canton rejected a CHF15.7m (£14.4m) planning credit, or budget allocation, for a project to renovate the museum's historic building and replace its 1983 extension, with 51.8% voting against it. The museum states its ageing buildings still urgently need repairs.

Sources indicate that schmidt succeeds Nina Zimmer, who led the institutions for a decade and will become director-general of Vienna's Belvedere in January 2027. The foundation’s commercial director Thomas Soraperra will serve as interim director until Schmidt arrives.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

What's your FI number? Calculate it in 60 seconds.

The one number that changes everything.

What $10,000 grows to at different rates over 30 years — the rate difference matters more than you think.

$10,000 invested for 30 years at 6% annual return.

$10,000 invested for 30 years at 8% annual return.

$10,000 invested for 30 years at 10% annual return.

Free calculators, a personalized FI roadmap, and a community of 25K+ on the same journey.

Future value (FV) is the projected worth of an investment at a specific point in the future, based on an assumed rate of growth. It answers the most practical question in investing: "If I invest this money today, what will it be worth in 10, 20, or 30 years?".

Future value calculations rest on compound interest — the principle that your returns earn their own returns over time. Albert Einstein reportedly called compound interest "the eighth wonder of the world," and while the attribution is debatable, the math is not. The difference between simple interest (returns on your original investment only) and compound interest (returns on your investment plus accumulated returns) becomes enormous over long time horizons.

The basic future value formula for a lump sum investment is:.

For example, $10,000 invested at 8% for 20 years:.

FV = $10,000 x (1.08)^20 = $10,000 x 4.661 = $46,610.

The table reveals two critical insights. First, small differences in return rates produce massive differences over long periods — $10,000 at 6% grows to $57,435 over 30 years, while the same amount at 10% grows to $174,494. That 4-percentage-point difference triples the outcome. Second, time is the dominant variable. At 8%, your money doubles roughly every 9 years — so 30 years gives you more than three doublings, turning $10,000 into over $100,000.

Most people do not invest a single lump sum and walk away. They invest regularly — monthly or per paycheck — over decades. The future value of a series of regular contributions uses a different formula called the future value of an annuity:.

FV = PMT x [((1 + r)^n - 1) / r].

Where PMT is the periodic contribution, r is the periodic rate, and n is the total number of periods.

In practice, you do not need to calculate this by hand. The insight that matters is this: regular contributions are far more powerful than most people realize because each contribution starts its own compounding clock. Your first $500 contribution compounds for the full 30 years, while your 360th contribution (at month 360) compounds for just one month — but together they build wealth that dwarfs a single lump sum.

A person investing $500 per month at 8% for 30 years accumulates $745,180 — from total contributions of only $180,000. That means $565,180, or 76% of the final balance, came from compound returns rather than your own deposits. This is the engine of wealth building.

In a recent development, every future value calculation should be done twice — once in nominal terms and once in real (inflation-adjusted) terms. The nominal return is the raw number your investments earn. The real return subtracts inflation, showing you what your money will actually buy.

Industry observers note that historically, the S&P 500 has returned roughly 10% nominally and 7% after inflation. The difference matters enormously over long periods:.

That $1.13 million in nominal terms has the purchasing power of roughly $610,000 in today's dollars — still excellent, but nearly half less than the headline number suggests. When planning for FI, always use real returns (6-7%) rather than nominal returns (9-10%) to avoid overestimating what your portfolio will actually support in retirement spending.

The Rule of 72 is the simplest and most useful mental math tool in investing. Divide 72 by your annual rate of return to estimate how many years it takes for your investment to double:.

In a recent development, this works in reverse too. If you want to know what rate of return you need to double your money in 15 years: 72 / 15 = 4.8%. The Rule of 72 is an approximation — it is most accurate for rates between 5% and 12% — but it is remarkably precise within that range and far faster than pulling out a calculator.

The FI community uses future value calculations as the backbone of retirement planning. The process works in three steps:.

The table reveals how starting balance and monthly contribution interact. Notice that increasing your monthly contribution from $1,500 to $2,500 (a $1,000 increase) with a $100,000 starting balance cuts 3.5 years off your time to $1 million. This is the savings rate lever in action — the amount you save each month matters more than any other variable you control.

A common question is whether it is better to invest a lump sum now or spread contributions over time (dollar-cost averaging). The math is clear: lump sum investing wins approximately two-thirds of the time because markets trend upward over the long term. However, dollar-cost averaging reduces the psychological risk of investing a large amount right before a downturn and provides a behavioral advantage that keeps many investors on track. For most FI-seekers, the question is academic — you invest each paycheck as it arrives because you do not have a large lump sum sitting on the sidelines.

Free calculators, a personalized FI roadmap, and a community of 25K+ on the same journey.

When projecting your portfolio growth for retirement planning, use real (inflation-adjusted) returns of 6-7% rather than nominal returns of 9-10%. A $1 million nominal balance in 30 years has the purchasing power of roughly $550,000 in today's dollars at 2% average inflation. Planning with real returns ensures you are targeting a portfolio that can actually support your desired spending level.

Track your actual spending for 3 months and annualize it. Multiply by 25 to get your FI number using the 4% safe withdrawal rate. If you spend $60,000 per year, your FI number is $1,500,000.

According to recent reports, add up all retirement accounts (401k, IRA, Roth IRA, HSA), taxable brokerage accounts, and savings. Exclude home equity and non-liquid assets. This is your starting balance for the future value calculation.

Subtract your monthly spending from your monthly after-tax income. Include employer 401(k) match and any other automatic savings. This is your periodic contribution amount for the future value formula.

Use the future value of a lump sum plus annuity formula, or a simple online calculator, to project when your current balance plus monthly contributions will reach your FI number. Use 7% real return (after inflation) for conservative planning.

According to recent reports, test what happens if you increase contributions by $200/month, $500/month, or $1,000/month. Seeing the concrete impact of a savings rate increase — often shaving 2-5 years off your FI timeline — makes the trade-offs tangible and motivating.

For long-term stock market projections, use 7% for inflation-adjusted (real) returns or 10% for nominal returns based on the S&P 500 historical average. For a more conservative estimate, use 6% real. For bond-heavy portfolios, use 3-4% real. Always specify whether you are using nominal or real returns — mixing them up is one of the most common planning mistakes.

Future value calculations show what WOULD happen if returns were constant every year. In reality, markets fluctuate — you might earn 25% one year and lose 15% the next. Over 20-30 year periods, average returns tend to converge toward historical norms, making future value projections reasonably useful for planning. Treat them as directional estimates, not guarantees.

Future value asks: "What will $10,000 today be worth in 20 years?" Present value asks the reverse: "What is $50,000 in 20 years worth in today's dollars?" They use the same variables but in opposite directions. Present value is useful for evaluating whether a future payout (like a pension or annuity) is worth the cost today.

It has been revealed that the Rule of 72 works for any compounding rate, including inflation. At 3% inflation, prices double every 24 years (72 / 3 = 24). This means $50,000 in annual spending today becomes $100,000 in 24 years in nominal terms — your purchasing power is halved if your income stays flat. This is why investing in assets that outpace inflation is essential.

For FI planning, future value is more intuitive — it tells you what your portfolio will grow to. However, the most practical approach is to calculate future value using real (after-inflation) returns. This effectively gives you a future value stated in today's purchasing power, which is what you actually need to know for spending planning.

Sources indicate that in tax-advantaged accounts (401k, IRA, Roth IRA, HSA), your investments compound without tax drag, so the standard future value formula works directly. In taxable accounts, capital gains taxes, dividend taxes, and tax-loss harvesting all affect your real return. A rough adjustment is to reduce your assumed return by 0.5-1.0% for taxable accounts to account for ongoing tax drag.

Future value calculations are the most practical tool in the FI planner's toolkit. They turn abstract concepts like compound growth and savings rate into concrete dollar amounts and specific timelines. The key takeaways are straightforward: use 7% real returns for conservative planning, always account for inflation by using real rather than nominal returns, and remember that your monthly contribution rate has a far larger impact on the outcome than chasing an extra point or two of return. The Rule of 72 gives you instant mental math for any investment decision — how long to double, what rate you need, and how inflation erodes purchasing power. Combined with a clear FI number and a disciplined savings rate, future value projections show you exactly when financial independence becomes reality. Run the numbers, test different scenarios, and let the math motivate you to increase that monthly contribution whenever you can.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The German government has agreed to hand over an extensive photo archive to the Jehovah’s Witnesses that documents the persecution of a pacifist Christian family under the Nazi regime.

Sources indicate that jehovah’s Witnesses were persecuted by the Nazis for their religious beliefs, particularly their refusal to serve in the military, pledge allegiance to Adolf Hitler, or participate in Nazi organizations. An estimated 4,500 Jehovah’s Witnesses were sent to concentration camps.

According to a report by The New York Times, among those persecuted were Franz and Hilda Kusserow and their 11 children, who lived in Bad Lippspringe, a town in the German state of North Rhine-Westphalia. Two of the couple’s sons were executed after refusing military service because of their religious beliefs. The three youngest children were taken from their family and placed in a Nazi training school, where they were prohibited from contacting their relatives. Both parents and their remaining children were sentenced to prison terms.

Sources indicate that one of their daughters Annemarie Kusserow was arrested by the Gestapo in October 1944 and remained a prisoner until May 25, 1945, after the war in Europe had ended. Over the following decades, Annemarie gathered and preserved a collection of more than 1,000 photographs, documents, drawings, letters, and reports documenting her family’s experiences.

In her 2005 will, Annemarie bequeathed the entire photo archive to the German headquarters of the Jehovah’s Witnesses. However, her brother Hans Werner Kusserow, to whom she had loaned the collection for research purposes, sold it to the Bundeswehr Military History Museum in Dresden, Germany, in 2009. The archive has remained in the German museum’s possession ever since.

Industry observers note that according to the Jehovah’s Witnesses’ official website, the sale of the photo collection to a military museum was “especially troubling” given that two of Annemarie’s brothers had lost their lives because of their pacifist beliefs. The organization says the sale of the archive “resulted in years of legal battles.”.

Sources indicate that the Jehovah’s Witnesses filed a lawsuit to recover the archive from the Bundeswehr Military History Museum, which is operated by the German armed forces. On November 19, the museum and the religious organization reached an “amicable agreement” under which the collection will be handed over to the Jehovah’s Witnesses. Both parties have agreed to keep the terms of the settlement confidential.

According to The Upcoming York Times, Sebastian Stock, a spokesman for the religious organization in Germany, notes that once the transfer is complete, the “Jehovah’s Witnesses will develop and present a concept for making the archive accessible for further academic research.”.

In addition to digitizing the archive and making it available to scholars, the Jehovah’s Witnesses initiative to display some of the documents in a fresh exhibition examining the history of the religious group in Central Europe.

Latest Update: Newly attributed Titian self-portrait, bought for almost $70,000 two years ago, on sale in London

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • “Both Rubens and his erstwhile assistant Van Dyck venerated Titian as the very prince of painters.” So writes the Titian expert Peter Humfrey in the catalogue for Dickinson’s impressive newly introduced exhibition, Titian, Rubens, Van Dyck, which opened last night and runs until 18th December at 58 Jermyn Street, London.
  • Sources indicate that simon Dickinson and his son Milo have brought together two paintings by Titian, two by Rubens and nine by Van Dyck for the show, all from private collections and most for sale, priced between around £400,000 and over £3m.
  • The exhibition, one of the most ambitious staged by the gallery in its 33-year history, is accompanied by an extensive catalogue including essays from Humfrey alongside the Belgian art historians Koenraad Jonckheere, a professor in Northern Renaissance and Baroque art at Ghent University, and Katlijne Van der Stighelen, a Rubens expert.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

“Both Rubens and his erstwhile assistant Van Dyck venerated Titian as the very prince of painters.” So writes the Titian expert Peter Humfrey in the catalogue for Dickinson’s impressive newly introduced exhibition, Titian, Rubens, Van Dyck, which opened last night and runs until 18th December at 58 Jermyn Street, London.

Sources indicate that simon Dickinson and his son Milo have brought together two paintings by Titian, two by Rubens and nine by Van Dyck for the show, all from private collections and most for sale, priced between around £400,000 and over £3m. At the heart of the show is the relationship between the three painters, principally the influence of Titian on the two younger, Flemish painters.

The exhibition, one of the most ambitious staged by the gallery in its 33-year history, is accompanied by an extensive catalogue including essays from Humfrey alongside the Belgian art historians Koenraad Jonckheere, a professor in Northern Renaissance and Baroque art at Ghent University, and Katlijne Van der Stighelen, a Rubens expert.

While works by Titian, Rubens and Van Dyck are “very, very difficult to find”, Milo Dickinson states, there are still some at large thanks to all three being extremely prolific. “Titian was this great role model to Rubens and then Van Dyck, both as a man who was a successful artist throughout his life, courted by major patrons, but also as a painter: the colours he used, the compositions he devised,” Dickinson says. Rubens, for instance, “spent several months just copying paintings by Titian in Madrid, which had been bought by Phillip II of Spain.” As for Van Dyck, the sketchbook he took around Italy when he was a young man is full of annotated studies of Titians.

The exhibition includes several recent rediscoveries, most made after cleaning, with the catalogue outlining the arguments in favour of the attributions made by various experts.

Peter Paul Rubens, Study of the young Anthony van Dyck (around 1616-7).

Recent findings suggest that courtesy: Simon C. Dickinson Ltd.

It has been revealed that among them is what is thought to be a late self-portrait by Titian, variously dated by scholars to between 1546-47 to 1560. The attribution has been long debated by scholars, Milo Dickinson says. Everett Fahy, the American art historian and former director of the Frick who died in 2018, first proposed the attribution to Titian in 2009 when the painting emerged—filthy—from a French private collection. The oil on canvas, small at 44cm by 33cm, was sold for $69,850 at Sotheby's Newly introduced York in 2024, catalogued as “attributed to Titian”. It has subsequently been cleaned, X-rayed and further studied. Now, Dickinson says, “various scholars—Peter Humfrey, Nicholas Penny and Ian Kennedy—have written on it and debated the dating of it because [if the attribution is correct] it would make it one of only three accepted self-portraits by Titian”, alongside those in the Gemäldegalerie in Berlin and that in the Prado, Madrid. The painting, which has been in a UK private collection since 2024, is now priced at £1.5m.

Industry observers note that another find is a Rubens head study which is now thought to depict a young Anthony van Dyck, based on dating, the sitter’s distinctive features and comparison with van Dyck’s self-portraits. The oil on panel, which measures 43cm by 35cm, was bought by the current owner at Sotheby’s Paris last November as part of the sale of the collection of the British property billionaire Manny Davidson. Catalogued as a Head Study of a Boy by Rubens, it sold for €744,000. With fitting circularity, Davidson had bought the painting as “attributed to Rubens” in 2007 from Simon Dickinson in 2007, who had spent several years trying to prove it was by Rubens.

According to recent reports, the study had been thought to date to around 1614, when Van Dyck would have been only 14 or 15 years old, younger than the boy depicted here with his wispy stubble. But the Louvre, which holds the other half of this double head study, has recently argued that its sketch probably dates to 1616-17. “That got us thinking,” Dickinson indicates. “Once you've seen it cleaned, you realise the hair colour, the distinct shape of the face, the lips, the shape of the nose, they're totally concurrent with what Van Dyck looked like in his self-portraits.” He adds that Jonckheere and Van der Stighelen support the identity of the sitter as being van Dyck, alongside other scholars. The head study is for sale, price undisclosed.

Brunaille equestrian study by van Dyck (around 1629-32).

According to recent reports, courtesy Simon C. Dickinson Ltd.

Industry observers note that yet another post-clean rediscovery is a study by van Dyck for the equestrian portrait of Albert de Ligne, Prince of Arenberg and Barbançon (around 1629-32) which hangs in Holkham Hall, Norfolk. It is one of several similar brunaille studies, one of which is the Metropolitan Museum of Art in Latest York. Another of these sketches, presumed to be the original, had been in the De Craecker collection in the 19th century but had since gone missing. “Then this one appeared in an American private collection and it was pretty clear, upon seeing it cleaned, that this was the original and the other versions were copies done in Van Dyck's studio by assistants.” Dickinson says.

He adds that “the sheer quality, the way that he uses highlights, the abbreviated forms” in this version are superior when compared to the others. The pentimenti (revisions) in this, typical of Van Dyck, have also become clearly visible over time, Dickinson notes, particularly the adjusted position of the horses head and front legs. The American collector, who bought it in 2014, is now selling the sketch through Dickinson, with an asking price in the region of £500,000.

At the top end of the price range is a friendship portrait by Titian, offered at £3m. Portrait of a young man with a gloved hand (around 1550) is thought to have been the portrait by Titian that is mentioned in van Dyck’s posthumous inventory. It was last publicly exhibited in 1939-40.

The exhibition will travel to New York for the Master Drawings New York art fair in (29 January–6 February 2027).

  • JKR rebuilds KFC around its bucket in the KFC Bucketverse: custom type, a redrawn Colonel, and a bucket that frames everything.
  • Industry observers note that the move is simple and hard to argue with.
  • Recent findings suggest that two custom typefaces carry the voice.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

JKR rebuilds KFC around its bucket in the KFC Bucketverse: custom type, a redrawn Colonel, and a bucket that frames everything.

Industry observers note that the move is simple and hard to argue with. Instead of inventing a upcoming symbol, JKR took the one object every KFC customer already knows and made it the system. The bucket is now a frame: it holds food photography, illustration and campaign lines, and it scales from a cup to a building. The logo itself turns three dimensional, the Colonel gets a warmer expression and a collar under his bow tie, and the red, white and black palette stays exactly where it was. Nothing about the brand gets thrown out. Everything gets pointed at the bucket.

Recent findings suggest that two custom typefaces carry the voice. Kentucky Fried Serif and Kentucky Fried Sans were drawn with StudioDRAMA, and the serif does the heavy lifting: it spells KFC at poster scale on the bucket, the bag and the building, with thick strokes and tight spacing that read from across a street. The stripes, once a background pattern, are reworked into a type-based asset that carries its own messages, and the boxes repeat lines like SUBSTANTIAL KFC FLAVOR DIALED UP TO 11 and NOTHING HITS LIKE KFC ORIGINAL CHICKEN in stacked red caps. Tobias Hall drew the Finger Lickin' Good lettering, which now works as a mark in its own right, set in script against the block serif.

Sources indicate that the system holds together because the same decisions repeat at every size. The kraft bag carries the serif wordmark at full height. The restaurant facade draws the bucket outline across the whole frontage in white line on red, with the Colonel sitting above the door. Inside, curved screens run giant red letterforms behind the counter, and the KWENCH drinks range gets its own vertical sign. A global roster of illustrators adds the colour: Bernardo Henning's loose, bright drawing fills the back of a black T-shirt, and a silver bucket pendant turns the packaging into jewellery. The photography follows the same rule, shot from inside the bucket looking up, so the food and the people sit inside the frame the brand built.

In a recent development, “Creators, such as photographers and image-makers, have little bargaining power against the might of significant tech,” Doran says in a statement. “We have been absolutely clear, creators’ work has been exploited without consent, and any Opt-Outs proposal, which has proven to be burdensome, should not be forced onto creators.

She warns that Australia’s ambitions to become more competitive in the AI sector should not come at the expense of creators’ rights.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Brightin Star first unveiled its fresh APO 35mm f/1.7 ASPH.
  • In a recent development, the Brightin Star 35mm f/1.7 APO ASPH.
  • In a recent development, although rangefinder-coupled with close focusing down to 0.7 meters (2.3 feet), the lens can focus as close as 0.3 meters (0.98 feet) when used in live view or adapted.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Brightin Star first unveiled its fresh APO 35mm f/1.7 ASPH. lens for Leica M-Mount cameras at CP+ in February and then launched it on Kickstarter in August. As of today, it’s available to everyone, and it’s still as handsome as ever.

In a recent development, the Brightin Star 35mm f/1.7 APO ASPH. is a full-frame, manual-focus lens with a native Leica M-Mount design. However, as evidenced by the fact that Brightin Star offers it in kits with E, Z, RF, X, L, and even GFX adapters, it’s easy to adapt to other camera systems. Although Brightin Star does not state the lens’s exact image circle when used with its GFX adapter, the company claims it covers the 44 x 33-millimeter sensor inside GFX system medium-format mirrorless cameras.

In a recent development, although rangefinder-coupled with close focusing down to 0.7 meters (2.3 feet), the lens can focus as close as 0.3 meters (0.98 feet) when used in live view or adapted. Brightin Star notes that 100 degrees of focus throw covers infinity to 0.7 meters, while an additional 207 degrees covers the relatively narrow distance from 0.3 to 0.7 meters. That 307 degrees of total focus rotation is quite a lot, and Brightin Star describes it as “cinema style.”.

Industry observers note that the 35mm f/1.7 prime is a compact, relatively lightweight lens. It measures just 43 millimeters (1.7 inches) long and weighs around 260 grams (9.2 ounces). It accepts 39mm front filters. Part of Brightin Star’s new “Apex” series of lenses, the 35mm f/1.7 APO ASPH. promises precision build quality and high-end optical performance.

In a recent development, “We believe a truly exceptional M-mount lens should never have to choose between heritage and innovation,” Brightin Star notes. “The Apex Series was created with this belief at its core. It preserves the timeless, understated character of classic M lenses while bringing together advanced optics, precision mechanics, and uncompromising standards of craftsmanship.”.

It has been revealed that on the topic of image quality, the lens features 11 elements arranged across seven groups. There are some notable elements inside, including three double-sided aspherical lenses, three high-refractive pieces of glass, and an ED element. There are also two floating lens groups that move independently during focusing, which the manufacturer indicates better controls distance-related aberrations and reduces spherical aberrations at close range. The lens also promises minimized focus breathing.

As evidenced by the “APO” in its name, Brightin Star indicates this is an “apochromatic” lens. While there’s no precise, industry-standard definition for what level of performance that requires, Brightin Star promises minimal chromatic aberration. An apochromatic lens focuses red, blue, and green wavelengths of light at the exact same point on the image plane. The closer a lens gets to achieving this ideal, the fewer chromatic aberrations it exhibits, all else being equal.

The Brightin Star MF 35mm f/1.7 APO ASPH. lens is available now for $1,099 for Leica M. An adapter adds $30, pushing the price to $1,129.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Hoor Al Qasimi, one of the preeminent figures of contemporary art in the Middle East, has been named curator of the Venice Biennale's next art exhibition, the Biennale has unveiled.

Following this year's edition, which was curated by the late Cameroon-born curator Koyo Kouoh, the appointment of Al Qasimi, from the United Arab Emirates (UAE), marks the second consecutive edition in which a woman from outside the Western art world has been chosen for the role.

Al Qasimi was born into the royal family of the port city of Sharjah and is the daughter of Sultan bin Muhammad Al Qasimi, the current leader of the emirate of Sharjah.

It has been revealed that she has been involved in the Sharjah Biennial since 2003, when she curated the exhibition's sixth edition after completing her undergraduate studies at the Slade School of Fine Art in London. In 2009, she founded the Sharjah Art Foundation, a public art organisation that promotes and funds contemporary art collaborations in the emirate and internationally, including organising the Sharjah Biennial.

In a recent development, she holds board positions for numerous other arts organisations, including the International Biennial Association, Sharjah Museums Authority, Sharjah Architecture Triennial and University of the Arts Sharjah. She has also curated major exhibitions including the Lahore Biennale in 2020, the Aichi Triennale in Japan in 2025, and this year's edition of the Biennale of Sydney.

Pietrangelo Buttafuoco, president of the Venice Biennale, claims in a statement that Al Qasimi's work gives “voice to stories and sensibilities shaped by research and the unexpected”.

He adds: “Her work brings together a profound attentiveness to deep-rooted memory and its legacies, an open perspective on the intricate complexities of the present, and a rare ability to listen to places and their people...These are qualities that we feel are particularly close to La Biennale’s vision”.

Buttafuoco, a right-leaning journalist and intellectual who was born and raised in Catania in Sicily, reportedly converted to Islam in 2015, adopting the name Giafar al-Siqilli (“Jafar the Sicilian”) in a reference to the Arab-Sicilian general associated with the Fatimid conquest of North Africa.

Since becoming president of the Biennale in 2024, he has sometimes championed art from the Middle East. In 2025, under his watch, Qatar revealed it would launch a national pavilion at the Biennale. A temporary structure was used for the most recent architecture and art biennales; the completed pavilion building will be the first permanent addition to the Giardini, one of the Biennale’s two main venues, in 30 years.

In a statement, Al Qasimi states that the Biennale “continues to be a critical space to engage with the work of influential artists and curators”, adding that she was “honoured” to be appointed as curator.

Al Qasimi could not immediately be reached for comment.

#173193. AI-Generated Characters Are Stealing Content Creators’ Viral Videos

📅 25 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 3m • 📚 Deep Dive (606 w)

AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Petapixel ↗ Open Full Page

AI-Generated Characters Are Stealing Content Creators’ Viral Videos

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (606 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Petapixel

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Content creators are increasingly discovering AI-generated versions of their videos in which almost everything is identical, except that they have been replaced by AI-generated characters.
  • From musicians and chefs to comedians, content creators are finding their performances copied by AI-generated characters that mimic their movements, jokes, and even the backgrounds in their original videos.
  • The phenomenon, known as “reskinning,” is becoming increasingly common across social media thanks to cheap and accessible AI tools.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Content creators are increasingly discovering AI-generated versions of their videos in which almost everything is identical, except that they have been replaced by AI-generated characters.

From musicians and chefs to comedians, content creators are finding their performances copied by AI-generated characters that mimic their movements, jokes, and even the backgrounds in their original videos.

The phenomenon, known as “reskinning,” is becoming increasingly common across social media thanks to cheap and accessible AI tools. People can take an existing video and replace the original performer with an artificial character, often designed to look funny, realistic, or hypersexualized.

The Instagram page More Perfect Union points to Higgsfield AI and its latest Genjutsu tool that allows owners to upload any video file and remix it with the user’s own character, locations, or product. However, other elements of the video remain untouched.

It has been revealed that just a few weeks ago, Nvidia invested in Higgsfield AI in a Series B funding round that raised $400 million. It gave Higgsfield a valuation of $5.4 billion.

A post shared by More Perfect Union (@perfectunion).

According to recent reports, sophie Lloyd, a U.K.-based guitarist who tours with U.S. rapper Machine Gun Kelly, tells the BBC she has spent years building an online following, only to see AI accounts reproduce content created by musicians and other performers.

“A lot [of these accounts] are getting thousands of views, thousands of followers, just for literally doing nothing and stealing the stuff that we’ve created,” Lloyd states.

Dr. Tina Kendall, an expert in online culture at Anglia Ruskin University, tells the British broadcaster that the practice is often less about experimentation with AI and more about exploiting content that has already demonstrated its popularity.

“What these tools allow people to do is just automatically take a viral concept that’s already existing and to reuse it through these reskinning tools,” she says.

While some accounts may use the technology for entertainment, Kendall says others are deliberately copying successful videos in the hope of attracting an audience and generating revenue.

Sources indicate that she sees the trend as part of a wider online “hustle culture,” in which accounts look to turn attention and engagement into money. That can mean directing followers toward subscription-based fan pages featuring adult content, promoting risky cryptocurrency products such as meme coins, or simply taking advantage of monetization features offered by social media platforms.

For the original creators, identifying and stopping the accounts responsible can be extremely difficult.

Alwyn Cruz, who has built a following on social media by exposing AI-generated musicians, describes trying to shut down these accounts as a game of whack-a-mole.

“You don’t even know who’s making these [videos]. And then if you shut it down, they’re just going to create another,” he notes.

Cruz states the problem extends well beyond musicians, with performers from a variety of disciplines finding their work replicated.

“It’s not only guitarists that are being cloned: there are drummers, taekwondo players that are being cloned, and I’ve seen this all over the internet.”.

The accessibility of AI reskinning tools like Higgsfield means the practice could become increasingly difficult to contain. Creators can spend years developing an online presence and refining a style that audiences recognize, only to find that the same performances can be reproduced with a different face and a few clicks.

And while the AI-generated versions may be attracting attention, the people behind the original performances are often left watching someone else benefit from their work.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • A family photographer has been arrested for allegedly hiding income from her photography business to obtain more than $30,000 in food assistance benefits.
  • Mary Miller, a 31-year-old Wisconsin-based family photographer who operated under the name Fawn Focus Photography, is facing multiple charges related to public assistance fraud.
  • Sources indicate that according to a long-term investigation by the Dodge County Sheriff’s Office in Juneau, Wisconsin, Miller allegedly failed to report her earnings as a self-employed photographer while claiming FoodShare and childcare assistance benefits over several years.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A family photographer has been arrested for allegedly hiding income from her photography business to obtain more than $30,000 in food assistance benefits.

Mary Miller, a 31-year-old Wisconsin-based family photographer who operated under the name Fawn Focus Photography, is facing multiple charges related to public assistance fraud.

Sources indicate that according to a long-term investigation by the Dodge County Sheriff’s Office in Juneau, Wisconsin, Miller allegedly failed to report her earnings as a self-employed photographer while claiming FoodShare and childcare assistance benefits over several years. FoodShare is Wisconsin’s food assistance program for individuals and families with limited incomes.

According to a report by Fox 11 News, an investigation was launched after Dodge County Economic Support uncovered apparent inconsistencies between Miller’s tax records, employment records, court documents, and applications for public assistance.

Authorities allege that the photographer provided inaccurate information about her income and residency when applying for benefits, including failing to disclose earnings from her business Fawn Focus Photography.

Between 2019 and 2025, Miller allegedly received more than $30,000 in FoodShare benefits that she was not entitled to claim. She also received more than $22,000 in childcare assistance benefits, although investigators were still determining how much of that funding was improperly obtained.

Sources indicate that according to online court records, Miller faces six counts of failing to disclose an event affecting her eligibility for benefits and six counts of failing to report the receipt of income or assets. The photographer made her initial court appearance this month and was issued a $5,000 signature bond.

Sources indicate that “Public assistance programs exist to help individuals and families during times of genuine need and are funded by hardworking taxpayers,” Dodge County Sheriff Dale J. Schmidt tells Fox 11 News in a statement. “When someone is alleged to have concealed income or provided false information in order to obtain benefits, it undermines public trust and diverts limited resources away from those who legitimately qualify for assistance.”.

Previously, PetaPixel reported on a photographer who was sentenced to five years in federal prison for defrauding a family out of $4.6 million and using $200,000 of the money to purchase Taylor Swift concert tickets. 46-year-old photographer Chanise Coyne was given jail time after pleading guilty to wire fraud over a multimillion-dollar fraud scheme involving fictional child modeling events.

Mondaine turns solar technology into design feature with Doppio Solar Skeleton timepiece

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Swiss watchmaker Mondaine has expanded its Doppio collection with the Solar Skeleton, a timepiece that brings solar technology into the foreground of its design.
  • Rather than concealing the solar plates beneath the dial, the watch reveals them through a precisely cut circular opening, turning a functional component into a defining visual feature.
  • The design builds on the distinctive visual language of Mondaine‘s Doppio collection, which is characterised by double-line hands and indexes, a concave dial and a double-domed sapphire crystal.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Swiss watchmaker Mondaine has expanded its Doppio collection with the Solar Skeleton, a timepiece that brings solar technology into the foreground of its design.

Rather than concealing the solar plates beneath the dial, the watch reveals them through a precisely cut circular opening, turning a functional component into a defining visual feature.

The design builds on the distinctive visual language of Mondaine‘s Doppio collection, which is characterised by double-line hands and indexes, a concave dial and a double-domed sapphire crystal.

Mondaine explained that these elements establish a sense of repetition, rhythm and structural clarity, while the exposed solar plates introduce an additional layer of depth and visual interest.

While solar technology is typically hidden from view, Mondaine has taken a different approach with the Doppio Solar Skeleton.

A carefully positioned circular opening around the centre of the dial offers a controlled view of the solar movement, while the outer section retains the indexes to ensure clear readability.

By making the technology visible, Mondaine aimed to bridge the watch’s technical function with its aesthetic identity, without compromising the “clarity and legibility” that define the collection.

Powered by a Swiss Ronda solar movement, the watch converts natural and artificial light into electrical energy, which is stored in a rechargeable battery.

According to Mondaine, a few minutes of sunlight can reactivate a fully discharged movement, while a full charge provides a power reserve of up to eight months in complete darkness.

The brand explained that this technology eliminates the need for regular battery replacements, offering a more resource-conscious approach to timekeeping.

The Doppio Solar Skeleton is available in two versions, each offering a different interpretation of its distinctive design.

The first combines a polished silver 316L stainless steel case with a vegan grape leather strap, bringing together traditional watchmaking materials and a contemporary material alternative.

The second features a polished black stainless steel case paired with a matching mesh bracelet, creating a more monochromatic appearance that emphasises the watch’s clean lines and geometric detailing.

Both versions feature a 41-millimetre case, a discreet date window and a precisely laser-etched Mondaine logo and solar markings.

A double-domed sapphire crystal and water resistance of up to 5 ATM complete the design, “combining refined aesthetics with everyday practicality”.

“With the Doppio Solar Skeleton, we wanted to make solar technology part of the design itself,” said Mondaine.

“By revealing the cells beneath the dial, we have created a watch where functionality becomes a defining aesthetic feature, while staying true to Mondaine’s principles of clarity, precision and Swiss design.”.

The Doppio Solar Skeleton reflects Mondaine’s commitment to iconic Swiss minimalist design, where form and function work together.

By integrating visible solar technology into the collection’s established design language, the watch intends to demonstrate how a functional element can become an integral part of a timepiece’s aesthetic identity.

To find out more about Mondaine and the Doppio Solar Skeleton, visit the brand’s website.

Hollywood and Analog Photography Power Kodak’s Fifth Consecutive Quarter of Growth

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (690 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Petapixel

💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has now been five straight quarters of growth for the transformed, resurgent Eastman Kodak.
  • After facing immense financial challenges for decades, including warnings about its ability to continue as a “going concern” last year, Eastman Kodak has risen from the ashes like a phoenix, cashing in on analog’s revival.
  • The star of the show for the Rochester, Fresh York-based Kodak is its Advanced Materials and Chemicals (AM&C) division, which posted 21% revenue growth in Q3 2026 compared to Q3 2025.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has now been five straight quarters of growth for the transformed, resurgent Eastman Kodak.

After facing immense financial challenges for decades, including warnings about its ability to continue as a “going concern” last year, Eastman Kodak has risen from the ashes like a phoenix, cashing in on analog’s revival.

The star of the show for the Rochester, Fresh York-based Kodak is its Advanced Materials and Chemicals (AM&C) division, which posted 21% revenue growth in Q3 2026 compared to Q3 2025. While AM&C’s $99 million in revenue is significantly less than Kodak’s $165 million in Print revenue, the Print division’s revenue actually dipped 7% year-over-year. In total, Kodak’s consolidated revenues of $276 million this past quarter are up 3%. Profits are up, too, increasing by 7%.

“Kodak delivered strong performance in the third quarter, once again achieving year-over-year improvement in revenue, gross profit and Operational EBITDA,” claims Jim Continenza, Kodak’s Executive Chairman and CEO, in SEC filings.

“We continue to execute our long-term plan and are seeing a return on our ongoing investments. Our primary growth engine, AM&C, is now our fastest-growing, most profitable unit. Our print business has performed well for the year to date despite challenging economic conditions. And, most importantly, we generated $27 million in cash for Q3, an vital indicator of the operational strength of our business. Looking forward, we’re focused on continuing to invest in our core businesses and finishing the year with profitable growth,” Continenza continues.

As Continenza claims, AM&C is Eastman Kodak’s fastest-growing and most profitable business unit. What exactly is AM&C, though? Kodak says AM&C covers the manufacturing of still, motion picture, and industrial films, plus specialty chemicals related to film, technologies, and medicine.

As CineD reports, in a call with investors, Continenza specifically called out the growing desire among Hollywood filmmakers to shoot their biggest projects on film.

“Film continues to be the capture medium of choice for major features,” Continenza told investors.

Industry observers note that while Christopher Nolan’s record-breaking IMAX epic, The Odyssey, made a lot of headlines for its use of over two million feet of film, it is just one example of the return of film to Hollywood. Kodak had a great story about The Odyssey in August that dug a bit deeper into the movie’s use of Kodak film.

Kodak says award-winning cinematographer and Director of Photography Hoyte van Hoytema used Kodak Vision3 250D 5207 for daytime exteriors and bright interiors, and Kodak Vision3 500T 5219 for low-light and night scenes.

It has been revealed that “The 250D and 500T are my sweet spot filmstocks. I love their grain structures and they’re very much my functional workhorses. The way I work with lenses, NDs, daylight and lights for night scenes, falls within the sensitivity curves of both those stocks. They are both versatile too. For example, I can shoot a little bit longer into magic hour with the 250D and I don’t have to resort too quickly into going higher-up in ASA,” van Hoytema told Kodak.

Earlier this year, Kodak celebrated seven movies shot on Kodak that competed for the Palme d’Or at Cannes 2026, and the legendary film company routinely updates its list of productions shot on film.

Paper Tiger, Disclosure Day, and Marty Supreme are just a few significant names on the list. Continenza also mentioned Sense and Sensibility and Digger in his call.

Industry observers note that then, of course, there’s Eastman Kodak’s growing still film business. Over the past year-plus, Eastman Kodak has brought photographic film sales back under its purview, rebranding many different stocks and even unveiling some latest, albeit familiar, ones. The company reintroduced some larger-format photo film stocks a few months ago, too.

In a recent development, between Hollywood’s reignited love affair with film and Eastman Kodak’s investment in both motion picture and still film production, it’s immediately evident that Eastman Kodak believes its path to future success goes through analog. The licensing deals for smash hit Kodak-branded products don’t hurt, either.

The astonishing, untold story of Marie-Anne “Baby” de Goldschmidt-Rothschild, who smuggled a Van Gogh painting and the artist's letters out of Nazi Europe

📅 27 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1761 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Theartnewspaper
