📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Among the early Van Gogh collectors was a young woman who had just turned 22. Born in 1892 to a very wealthy German family, Marie-Anne (nicknamed “Baby”) de Goldschmidt-Rothschild certainly had the money, but also avant-garde taste. She bought one of the artist’s finest portraits.

Her amazing story is told in a meticulously researched fresh book: A Collector’s Odyssey: How Marie-Anne de Goldschmidt-Rothschild saved her Paintings from Nazi Looting, written by Christel Force, Anna-Carolin Augustin and Katharina Weiler and published in Berlin by De Gruyter (it is freely downloadable).

Van Gogh’s The Arlésienne (November 1888).

Sources indicate that musée d’Orsay, Paris (Donation sous réserve d'usufruit Mme R. de Goldschmidt-Rothschild, 1952 © photo : RMN-Grand Palais (Musée d’Orsay) / Stéphane Maréchalle).

Sources indicate that it may come as a surprise that the very first painting bought by Marie-Anne (whose maiden name was Friedländer-Fuld) was a Van Gogh - and an important one. Encouraged by progressive mentors, in June 1914 she purchased The Arlésienne (November 1888), a portrait of the artist’s friend Marie Ginoux, co-owner of the Café de la Gare in Arles. The picture cost the equivalent of £6250, a very large sum for a Van Gogh at the time. (There is another version at Upcoming York’s Metropolitan Museum of Art).

Marie-Anne later recounted how she hung the portrait, on antique-gold wallpaper, in her suite in the family’s palatial residence in Berlin’s Pariser Platz, almost next to the Brandenburg Gate: “My first and only painting, at the centre [of her main room], dominating everything and everyone, was L’Arlésienne by Van Gogh”. Her father, who had much more traditional tastes, abhorred the artist, telling her to hide “the jaundiced old lady” behind a curtain.

Marie-Anne de Goldschmidt-Rothschild, with her Louis XV sofa and Van Gogh’s The Arlésienne in her Berlin mansion (1929).

Photograph by Ernst Schneider, De Querschnitt journal (Berlin), September 1929.

Industry observers note that this was only the beginning. Marie-Anne went on to collect other Impressionist artists and their followers: Paul Gauguin, Claude Monet, Pierre-Auguste Renoir, Edouard Manet, Paul Cezanne and Pablo Picasso.

Sources indicate that by the time Marie-Anne was 31, she had married three times: to the English aristocrat John Mitford, the former German foreign minister Richard von Kühlmann and the aristocratic banker Rudolf von Goldschmidt-Rothschild (he used “von”, while she preferred “de”). After a few years, she and Rudolf lived independently and eventually divorced in 1938.

With the rise of the Nazis, Marie-Anne, who was of Jewish heritage, smuggled the Van Gogh portrait twice. The first time was in 1934, a year after Hitler came to power, when she secretly sent the painting from Berlin to her residence in Paris. This required subterfuge: she commissioned an artist friend, Eugen Spiro, to paint identical copies of her most important paintings. The copy of The Arlésienne was then surreptitiously placed in the frame in her Berlin mansion, with no one apparently noticing the switch.

The Van Gogh and the other canvasses were taken off their stretchers and rolled up. Marie-Anne instructed Marie-Anne instructed her (female) servants to each carry a single roll to Paris, without telling them what was inside. Had the pictures been declared at the border, Nazi officials would have prevented them from being exported or would have charged her an exorbitant tax. The Arlésienne safely arrived at Marie-Anne's mansion in Paris on the Rue de la Faisanderie.

Recent findings suggest that six years later, France was threatened by Germany. In mid-May 1940, a month before the Nazi occupation of Paris, Marie-Anne decided to flee to the US, protecting her life and collection. By that time, the only route was via Portugal, which was neutral. In a move which the book’s co-author Force describes as “reckless and admirable in equal measure”, Marie-Anne hatched a strategy for her most vital paintings.

She took the canvases strapped to the roof of her Citroën. Amidst the chaos of millions fleeing Paris, she drove across France to Spain, facing seemingly endless logistical challenges, but eventually reaching Portugal. Although some reports suggest the Van Gogh was transported on the roof with the rest of the paintings, Marie-Anne later told a different story.

According to her, The Arlésienne had been sent earlier to Amsterdam, on loan for an exhibition. Just one week before the German invasion in May 1940, her contact in the Netherlands somehow managed to get the Van Gogh onto an aircraft bound for Lisbon.

It has been revealed that in her hotel room in Portugal, Marie-Anne rolled up all her paintings, although the thick impasto paint of The Arlésienne created problems. She then covered the whole roll with a protective tarpaulin. Eventually she secured a place on a liner crossing the Atlantic, bound for Mexico.

After her ship finally arrived at Veracruz, Marie-Anne travelled on to Mexico City, later taking a plane to Texas and another flight on to Latest York, accompanied by her paintings. The Arlésienne had been travelling during wartime for nearly five months, arriving in New York in November 1940.

Marie-Anne, thanks to her immense wealth and elite contacts, had managed to escape the terrible fate of the vast majority of continental European Jewry.

In 1928, Marie-Anne made another prescient purchase: a collection of 22 letters written by Van Gogh in 1887-89 to his artist friend Emile Bernard (plus one to Gauguin). The bulk of Vincent’s surviving letters remained with Theo and his heirs, so the Bernard correspondence represented a very key acquisition. Many of the letters also included small sketches of the paintings which Van Gogh was working on.

Van Gogh’s letter to Emile Bernard, around 19 June 1888 (extracts).

Van Gogh Museum, Amsterdam (Vincent van Gogh Foundation).

In a recent development, when the art lover and writer Harry Kessler visited Marie-Anne in 1929, he noted in his diary that they had dined under The Arlésienne. Kessler then recorded: “After dinner, thirty letters by Van Gogh in an excessively ornate, ugly binding, were passed around with cigarettes and coffee.” (Although Kessler remarked it was 30 letters, it was actually 23.) Contrasting the opulence with the artist’s simple way of life, Kessler added: “Poor Van Gogh!”.

In 1940, when Marie-Anne fled from Paris in her Citroën, she carried this ornately-bound volume of Van Gogh’s correspondence in a suitcase. She kept the letters during her American wartime exile.

Recent findings suggest that on 26 August 1944, just hours after Paris was liberated, Marie-Anne wrote from California to the Free France delegation in Washington, DC: “My hand is shaking with emotion as I am writing to you today, day of the Liberation of Paris. I turn to you to ask that whoever is concerned be informed that I bequeath my Van Gogh painting L’Arlésienne to the city of Paris. It is at the Louvre, I expect, that it will find its place.”.

Marie-Anne left Upcoming York and returned to Europe in 1947, once again taking her paintings with her. Her family’s palatial residence in Berlin had been almost totally destroyed by Allied bombs, and she wanted to settle in her mansion in Paris. There she would spend the rest of her life, until her death in 1973.

The dining room in Marie-Anne de Goldschmidt-Rothschild’s Paris mansion (1950s).

Photograph by Antoinette Georges Perrier, De Goldschmidt-Rothschild family archive.

Marie-Anne had lived with The Arlésienne for nearly 60 years. After her death, the painting went to the Louvre, which displayed it in the Jeu de Paume. It was transferred to the Musée d’Orsay when it opened in 1986.

We can report that next year The Arlésienne will be presented in an exhibition at the Musée de l’Orangerie in Paris: Dépossédes: Oeuvres spoliées, vies brisées 1933-45 (Dispossessed: Plundered Art, Shattered Lives 1933–45)(October 2027-January 2028). Marie-Anne’s life certainly had its challenges, but it was hardly shattered like most of the other collectors who will be featured in the show.

Industry observers note that as for the Van Gogh correspondence, Marie-Anne donated one letter to the Fondation Custodia in Paris, another somehow left her collection and the one addressed to Gauguin was given to a friend. This left 20 letters which she bequeathed to her grandson, Frédéric de Goldschmidt-Rothschild. He sold the group to the New York dealer and collector Eugene Thaw in 2001.

Thaw later recalled how he bought the letters: “A young man [the grandson] showed up in my office with them all under his arm—unframed, unmatted—in a simple folder. And of course I nearly died of pleasant shock at seeing them.” Marie-Anne’s ornate binding had already gone.

It has been revealed that the correspondence was generously donated by Thaw to New York’s Morgan Library & Museum. These vital Van Gogh letters, with their 14 sketches, are now reunited online with the rest of the artist’s correspondence.

According to recent reports, for conservation reasons, Van Gogh's letters to Bernard are very rarely exhibited, but I once had the privilege of examining the originals in the Morgan’s study room. Seeing the letters, penned by the artist on ordinary writing paper with his little sketches, I thought back to when they had once been housed in Marie-Anne’s ornate album—and their perilous journey during the war.

Martin Bailey is a leading Van Gogh specialist and special correspondent for The Art Newspaper. He has curated exhibitions at the Barbican Art Gallery, Compton Verney/National Gallery of Scotland and Tate Britain.

Martin Bailey’s recent Van Gogh books.

Martin has written a number of bestselling books on Van Gogh’s years in France: The Sunflowers Are Mine: The Story of Van Gogh's Masterpiece (Frances Lincoln 2013, UK and US), Studio of the South: Van Gogh in Provence (Frances Lincoln 2016, UK and US), Starry Night: Van Gogh at the Asylum (White Lion Publishing 2018, UK and US) and Van Gogh’s Finale: Auvers and the Artist’s Rise to Fame (Frances Lincoln 2021, UK and US). The Sunflowers are Mine (2024, UK and US) and Van Gogh’s Finale (2024, UK and US) are also now available in a more compact paperback format.

According to recent reports, his other recent books include Living with Vincent van Gogh: The Homes & Landscapes that shaped the Artist (White Lion Publishing 2019, UK and US), which provides an overview of the artist’s life. The Illustrated Provence Letters of Van Gogh has been reissued (Batsford 2021, UK and US). My Friend Van Gogh/Emile Bernard provides the first English translation of Bernard’s writings on Van Gogh (David Zwirner Books 2023, UKand US).

YouTube Is Suddenly Obsessed With Views

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that this year, YouTube has changed how it counts views twice — and both occurred within three months of each other, which is shifting the paradigm of expectations for creators and advertisers. It also appears both creepy and desperate on YouTube’s part.

The first adjustment came back in August when YouTube changed when it would count a view, separating the metric into two parts: a standard view as well as an engaged view.

Industry observers note that “A view is now defined as counting from the very first frame — whether that’s a Short appearing in the feed or a long-form video autoplaying on the Home page,” YouTube explains. “An engaged view is defined as clicking to watch or watching past the initial seconds. This has been, and will continue to be, how you qualify to earn (as long as the content is also public).”.

According to recent reports, that engaged view is basically what standard, public views were before the change and remains in place because YouTube wanted to make its view numbers appear larger to the public, but it also didn’t want to have to tie creator payouts to those higher numbers. Basically, YouTube wanted to have its cake and eat it, too.

YouTube notes it changed the way it counts public views because it wanted to standardize metrics across formats and therefore measure audience reach more accurately. In short, because Meta and TikTok count views instantly on short-form content, YouTube felt like its view numbers on long-form content weren’t keeping up with the times.

This does, at least from YouTube’s perspective, make sense. Short-form has become a huge part of how people consume content now, for better or for worse. While YouTube Shorts are not nearly as popular as Instagram Reels or TikTok, YouTube does have them, and separating how it counted views there to be in line with the competition without adjusting them on long-form felt disjointed.

Industry observers note that it’s the second view change YouTube made in 2026 that feels, as I remarked at the top, particularly creepy and desperate. Starting earlier this month, YouTube started estimating how many people are in the room with a viewer when they play a video on a television and counting those estimations toward the public view count.

Sources indicate that “TVs are usually shared devices where friends, families, and communities come together to watch their favorite content. Until now, one TV playback has only counted as a single public view, even if several people watched together on the same living room screen. By updating public view counts to include co-views, we’re solving this measurement gap, better aligning with long-standing TV industry standards, and telling a more accurate story of how viewers watch your content,” YouTube states.

When first hearing how YouTube is approaching this, it sounds like YouTube is finding some way to actually see into living rooms. YouTube says this isn’t the case and it doesn’t actually know how many people are sitting in front of the television. Instead, it uses a video’s genre, audience demographics, and the time of day to guess. If YouTube thinks the video attracts a group and it is being watched in the evening, it will use that data to estimate more than one viewer.

“Co-view rate works as a ratio to show how estimated co-views contribute to your overall public views. For example, a Co-view rate of 1.10 means that for every 1,100 views of a video on TV, 1,000 are primary views from the device playback and 100 come from co-viewing,” YouTube explains.

Okay, sure, but why? It just seems like YouTube is obsessed with increasing its view counts to pump up how the platform is perceived while simultaneously not giving creators anything new. None of these changes actually affect revenue for YouTubers.

“This change only updates public view counts. Your actual creator earnings, ad revenue splits, and YouTube Partner Program (YPP) requirements remain unchanged,” YouTube stipulates regarding co-views.

According to recent reports, that’s the part that really stands out. Sure, not giving more revenue based on the latest calculation of a standard view from August makes sense. That’s not an additional person or viewer more than before; it’s just a new way of deciding at what point the view starts. Fine.

But if co-views are calculating additional people, there is no reason why those views shouldn’t count toward earned revenue. Those are, factually, additional human eyes seeing those videos.

Instead, YouTube gets to pitch advertisers on massive living-room reach while paying creators strictly on single-device clicks. Until those estimated eyeballs translate into actual ad revenue, co-views feel less like a win for creators and more like creative accounting designed to make YouTube look bigger than it is.

I guess when investors are demanding constant growth and the number of humans whose eyes can actually watch content does eventually reach a finite point, the only option is to just make up more eyes.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Koto's De-extinction brand identity turns compostable packaging into a protest, with loud dinosaurs, acid green and hot pink.

Industry observers note that the dinosaurs are back as warnings. Koto draws them in thick black outlines and fills them with acid green and hot pink, then sets them loose across kraft cups, stickered boxes and poster walls. The palette is deliberately loud: acid green, hot magenta, black and off-white, with the brown of the compostable board keeping the whole system grounded. The posters shout in stacked capitals, Sweet packaging without the sour aftertaste and Re-package your future, while the product photography drops the cups into a lush jungle world of flowers, rock and mist. Koto calls the idea Once Upon A Time, and even created the De-extinction name, a reminder that extinction is real unless we act.

The type does the shouting. A heavy grotesque runs at poster scale in tight stacked lines, with single words reversed out of black bars: FEED and NOURISH picked out in white on black, PLANET highlighted in pink. The de-extinction wordmark stays small and lowercase beside a round dino mark, letting the headlines carry the volume. The same bluntness holds where the system has to be practical: a catalog page lists cold cup sizes in a plain table under a giant COLD CUPS header, with a small dino doodle at the foot.

Sources indicate that the packaging is the proof. Kraft cups carry the small dino mark, boxes arrive covered in dino stickers, and a paper bag sits in the jungle photography with the same mark. Nothing is coated in gloss: the board stays brown, the print stays flat, and the dinosaurs do the talking. Koto took its cue from protest culture and global movements, building the brand to provoke action rather than nod at it, and the identity runs the same way across packaging, posters and communications. The approach landed: the identity helped the young company stand out with key customers, including meetings with Sweetgreen.

See more from Koto on the De-extinction project page.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The category winners for the Illume Awards have been revealed, an extreme sports photography competition built on the legacy of Red Bull Illume.

For 20 years, Red Bull turned the Illume Awards into the most recognizable competition for adventure and action sports photography.

Recent findings suggest that this year, it is just the Illume Awards. But the breathtaking images keep coming; check out this year’s category winners below.

French photographer Louis Garnier has won the Snow Category of The Illume Awards 2026 with his photo of skier Kevin Rolland captured in front of a fire fountain in Tignes, France.

Industry observers note that “The energy around the whole project was incredible. We only had three attempts with the flames, and it is still my favorite photo I’ve ever made with Kevin”, he recounts about the day the winning photo was taken.

Austrian photographer Tom Klocker takes the title in the Climb Category with his photograph of climber Mario Andexlinger in Iceland, selected as the winning image from 20 Climb Category Finalists.

Industry observers note that “This shot was very challenging, and you had to have extremely good ice climbing experience. The mystical atmosphere that day went perfectly with the colors,” says Klocker about the making of the photograph.

French photographer Tim Rochas has won the Aerial Category of The Illume Awards 2026 with his photograph of paraglider Pierre Bottero flying alongside Factory Butte in Utah, United States.

Captured from another glider in flight, the image places the pilot against the vast, rugged desert landscape, creating a striking contrast between the scale of nature and the small human presence in the air.

In a recent development, the story behind the winning photograph began with a flight from the top of Factory Butte. As the pilots took to the air above the extraordinary desert landscape, Rochas saw an opportunity to capture Bottero alongside the immense rock formation.

“For me, this image is about the contrast between the fragility of a human in flight and the raw power of nature,” he states.

Portuguese photographer Beatriz Ryder is the winner of the Surf Category of The Illume Awards 2026. Her photograph of surfer Shaley Mercado in the Solomon Islands was selected as the winning image from 20 Surf Category Finalists.

“We were in one of the most remote parts of the world, the Solomon Islands. Right in front of where we were staying was this little wave – shallow, fast, and with short, fun runners,” states Ryder about the location behind her winning photograph.

Spanish photographer Ágata Dominguez has won the Trail Category of The Illume Awards 2026 with her captivating photo of late athlete Ida Amelie Robsahm captured in Sancti Spiritu, Spain, during the Zegama-Aizkorri Race 2026, a legendary trail running race.

It has been revealed that “What I love most about photography is being there for the moments that are difficult to explain afterwards, capturing that look, that movement, and that energy in a split second: the tension, the concentration, and the feeling of being completely immersed in what’s happening. I’m not just interested in getting the perfect shot; I would like my images to make you feel something and, ideally, make you feel like you were there,” she explains her approach to photography.

German photographer Robert Christ takes the title in the Skate Category with his photograph of skater André Gerlich in Germany, selected as the winning image from 20 Skate Category Finalists.

Robert Christ’s photo captures André Gerlich performing a backside air trick on a sculpture by Andreas Kiessling in southern Germany.

“André and I found out about a sculpture bike path and immediately made plans to go there. André chose to skate this rough piece of concrete, did a stylish backside air, and we got a photo we were both really stoked about,” Christ claims.

American photographer Lear Miller has won the Bike Category of The Illume Awards 2026 with his photograph of Hannah Bergemann, captured as part of Chris Benchetler’s Mountains of the Moon project in Pacific City, Oregon, United States.

Industry observers note that getting the photo was not easy, as Miller explains, “We shot the bike segment of Chris Benchetler’s Mountains of the Moon over four nights, from about 10 pm to 4 am, in some pretty brutal rain. The riders were riding in the dark while we constantly battled water on the lenses and gear.”.

Chilean photographer Gonzalo Robert Parraguez has been named the winner of the Adventure Category of The Illume Awards 2026 with his photograph of kayaker Aniol Serrasolses in Svalbard, Norway.

The photo captures Aniol Serrasolses descending a waterfall in the Norwegian archipelago of Svalbard.

“We always talk about the photo, but we rarely talk about the athletes, and I dedicate this 100% to Aniol; he was the one who pushed for this whole project to happen, so that we could be taking these incredible photos in the middle of the Arctic”, says Parraguez.

For more on the contest, head to the Illume Awards website.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A will (technically a "last will and testament") is a legal document that specifies how your assets should be distributed after your death. It must go through probate — a court-supervised process that validates the will, pays debts and taxes, and distributes assets to beneficiaries. A living trust (specifically a revocable living trust) is a legal entity you create during your lifetime that holds your assets. When you die, the successor trustee distributes those assets according to the trust terms — without court involvement.

The critical distinction is probate. In states with expensive or slow probate processes — California, New York, Florida, and many others — a living trust pays for itself many times over. In states with simplified probate procedures (like Texas or Wisconsin for small estates), the cost advantage of a trust is smaller but the privacy and incapacity benefits still apply.

You need both: A trust does not name guardians for minor children (only a will can do that), and a trust only controls assets that have been formally transferred into it. A pour-over will acts as a safety net — it directs any assets not in the trust at your death to pour into the trust, where they are distributed according to the trust terms. The pour-over will still goes through probate, but it ensures nothing falls through the cracks.

The term "living trust" almost always refers to a revocable living trust — one you can change, amend, or dissolve at any time during your lifetime. You remain the trustee, manage the assets as you always have, and pay taxes on trust income using your personal Social Security number. For income tax purposes, a revocable trust is invisible — the IRS treats it as if it does not exist.

Sources indicate that an irrevocable trust is fundamentally different. Once established, you cannot easily modify it, and the assets inside it are no longer legally yours. This permanence provides two powerful advantages:.

Sources indicate that the federal estate tax exemption is $13.61 million per person ($27.22 million for married couples) in 2026, but this historically high exemption is scheduled to sunset after 2025, potentially dropping to approximately $7 million per person. FIRE households who have built $3 million to $10 million in net worth through decades of saving and investment growth should monitor this sunset closely. If the exemption drops, irrevocable trusts become relevant at much lower wealth levels.

For most FIRE households with $1 million to $5 million in net worth, a revocable living trust provides the right balance of control, flexibility, and probate avoidance. Irrevocable structures become compelling only when estate tax exposure is real or asset protection needs are elevated.

Estate planning is governed primarily by state law, and the value of a living trust versus a will varies significantly depending on where you live.

Sources indicate that nine states are community property states: Arizona, California, Idaho, Louisiana, Nevada, Fresh Mexico, Texas, Washington, and Wisconsin. In these states, most assets acquired during marriage are owned 50/50 by both spouses regardless of whose name is on the title. At death, only the deceased spouse's half passes through their estate strategy.

It has been revealed that the remaining 41 states follow common law (also called "equitable distribution"). Ownership depends on whose name is on the title. This distinction affects how assets pass at death and whether a trust or will provides better spousal protection.

It has been revealed that remember that a trust only controls assets titled in the trust's name. After creating a trust, you must fund it by re-titling your bank accounts, brokerage accounts, and real estate into the trust. Unfunded trusts — trusts that exist on paper but hold no assets — provide zero benefit. The pour-over will catches stragglers, but relying entirely on the pour-over defeats the purpose because those assets still go through probate.

Free calculators, a personalized FI roadmap, and a community of 25K+ on the same journey.

Recent findings suggest that the most common estate planning mistake with trusts is failing to fund them. Creating a trust document costs $1,500 to $5,000, but if you never transfer your bank accounts, brokerage accounts, and real estate into the trust, it provides zero probate avoidance. After signing your trust, immediately re-title assets into the trust name. Your attorney should provide a funding checklist. An unfunded trust sitting in a drawer is an expensive piece of paper — not an estate strategy.

According to recent reports, yes. A pour-over will catches any assets not transferred into your trust during your lifetime and directs them into the trust at death. A will is also the only legal document that can name guardians for minor children. Every trust-based estate plan should include a pour-over will.

Sources indicate that A revocable living trust prepared by an estate planning attorney typically costs $1,500 to $5,000, depending on complexity and your location. This usually includes the trust document, pour-over will, powers of attorney, healthcare directives, and initial funding guidance. Online trust services cost $200 to $500 but may not address state-specific concerns or complex situations.

In a recent development, yes, and you should be. With a revocable living trust, you serve as both the grantor (creator) and the trustee (manager). You maintain full control over all trust assets during your lifetime. You name a successor trustee who takes over only if you become incapacitated or die.

It has been revealed that A revocable living trust does not reduce estate taxes — the IRS treats it as if it does not exist for income and estate tax purposes. However, a trust can be structured with provisions (such as an A/B trust or disclaimer trust) that maximize the use of both spouses' estate tax exemptions. For estate tax reduction, irrevocable trusts are the primary tool.

A revocable trust can be changed, amended, or dissolved at any time. You maintain full control. An irrevocable trust generally cannot be changed after creation, and the assets inside it are no longer legally yours. Revocable trusts provide probate avoidance and incapacity planning. Irrevocable trusts provide estate tax reduction and asset protection.

Without a trust, each state where you own real property requires a separate probate proceeding (called ancillary probate), multiplying costs and complexity. Transferring out-of-state property into a living trust eliminates ancillary probate entirely — the successor trustee can transfer or sell the property without court involvement in any state.

It has been revealed that the living trust vs will decision is not about which is better — it is about which is better for your specific situation. For estates with more than $100,000 in probatable assets, especially in high-cost probate states, a revocable living trust saves thousands of dollars and months of delay while providing incapacity protection and privacy that a will cannot match. For smaller estates in simplified-probate states, a well-drafted will with proper beneficiary designations may be all you need. Either way, the worst estate proposal is no estate plan. More than 60% of American adults have neither a will nor a trust, leaving their families to navigate probate without guidance, pay avoidable costs, and endure unnecessary delays during the most difficult time of their lives.

Missouri has opened an investigation into a photography business after allegedly leaving numerous customers without the pictures they paid for or a refund.

According to a report by First Alert 4, Leave It to Beaver Photography — a professional family, newborn and wedding photography business based in Wentzville, Missouri — confirmed it had closed this week after 13 years in business.

Sources indicate that however, numerous customers have contacted First Alert 4 with complaints about the firm. Some allege they paid for photography services covering events such as weddings, births and anniversaries, but never received their photographs or a refund.

Industry observers note that kristen Moran alleges she hired Leave It to Beaver Photography to take family photographs during a Memorial Day weekend camping trip. She also contracted the tech giant for a maternity shoot in July.

Moran said the photographs were supposed to be delivered within 20 days, but they did not arrive as promised.

Industry observers note that “It came to months and months of her saying oh I have them, don’t worry about it. Just kind of getting the runaround,” Moran tells the news outlet.

Moran said the photographs eventually arrived in late October, but by then she had already given birth and no longer needed the maternity images.

In a recent development, “Late October she did send me the photos. She sent me like 300 of them. I was like okay, great. They’re not really relevant anymore, I already had my baby,” Moran notes.

In another case, Monica Dannegger alleges she hired Leave It to Beaver Photography to photograph her wedding on December 12, 2026. Dannegger says she paid the business $1,500, representing half the cost of photographing her wedding and an engagement party. However, she alleges the photographer did not attend the engagement party and that she has received no communication about the wedding. Dannegger also says she has been unable to obtain a refund.

“It’s unfortunate that her end of the bargain isn’t being upheld,” Dannegger tells First Alert 4. “I would have been left high and dry.”.

According to recent reports, the Missouri attorney general has reportedly opened an investigation into the photography business, which operates in St. Charles County. The office is encouraging customers who believe they have been affected to file a complaint through its website. Wentzville police have also advised customers who paid for services they did not receive to file a police report. Officers say they will investigate.

First Alert 4 says it had contacted Leave It to Beaver Photography for comment but had been unable to reach the photographer.

The news comes a wedding photographer was ordered to pay $1.7 million by the North Carolina Attorney General after leaving hundreds of customers without the services they paid for.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Roboto Studio rebuilt the Flowhub brand identity around one mark, Helvetica Now and Neon Moss green, from the website to the checkout screen.

Flowhub runs point of sale, payments, ecommerce, marketing and reporting for specialty retailers across the United States, from cannabis dispensaries to liquor stores and CBD shops. More than $4B in sales passes through it every year. Its old purple identity is gone. In its place, Roboto Studio built a system on a single mark, one typeface and one bright green, then carried the same parts into the website and the product interface, so the homepage, the dashboard and the payment screen at the counter are made from the same pieces. The line that runs through it all indicates it plainly: Retail moves fast. We move faster.

Helvetica Now does the talking. Display Bold carries the headlines at sizes that fill the frame, white on Rich Black, while Display Medium, Text Medium and Text Regular step down through the interface without changing voice. The specimen page lines the weights up beside a full character set, and the restraint shows in how little else the layouts need. The mark is a compact flowing form that reads at a glance and crops into a poster motif at bus stop scale. On the homepage the grid keeps real product screens in view, a strip of retailer logos leading into the hardware and apps, Maui OS, ecommerce, kiosk and delivery, each shown as the actual screen.

According to recent reports, two materials carry the system. Liquid chrome gives the mark its weight, a molten rendering that turns up on the poster, the SOC 2 shield and the map of backers. Frosted glass does the quieter work, layering the interface panels, the one platform stack and the deal cards Max drafts over photography. Color stays disciplined. Pearly White and Rich Black cover most of every surface, Pearl holds the panels, Neon Moss appears only on the one action that matters, and Sunburst orange is kept for anything that needs attention. The Intelligence dashboard opens on what needs attention today, sales, margin and stock value at the top, with Max drafting a reorder before a bestseller runs out. At the counter, the payment screen turns fully Neon Moss with a single word, Paid, large enough to read from the customer side.

See the full project on Roboto Studio's website.

How a Photographer Got a Credit on Jennifer Lopez’s Instagram Account

📅 27 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (776 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Petapixel

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A photographer has revealed how he managed to get a credit on Jennifer Lopez’s Instagram account after the star initially reposted his video without any attribution.
  • Los Angeles-based David Christopher Lee has been a celebrity portrait photographer for 27 years, capturing stars like Lady Gaga, the Kardashians, and Britney Spears.
  • Industry observers note that on November 19, Lee attended the premiere of Jennifer Lopez’s The JLo Show at Paramount Studios in Hollywood as a guest of his friend Maximillian Acevedo.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A photographer has revealed how he managed to get a credit on Jennifer Lopez’s Instagram account after the star initially reposted his video without any attribution.

Los Angeles-based David Christopher Lee has been a celebrity portrait photographer for 27 years, capturing stars like Lady Gaga, the Kardashians, and Britney Spears.

A post shared by Jennifer Lopez (@jlo).

Industry observers note that on November 19, Lee attended the premiere of Jennifer Lopez’s The JLo Show at Paramount Studios in Hollywood as a guest of his friend Maximillian Acevedo. Lee indicates he had no intentions of taking any photographs or videos at the event.

In a recent development, however, when Lopez came out on the red carpet, photographers rushed out to take pictures, and Lee couldn’t resist shooting some images of the star herself. Lee moved behind the crowd of photographers to find a different angle of Lopez. He noticed Lopez’s yellow diamond necklace and zoomed in to capture a 13-second video on his iPhone at 5x zoom.

The lighting was particularly good, illuminating Lopez’s jawline and earring, and Lee says he immediately knew he had captured the shot he wanted.

Sources indicate that “As all the photographers started calling her name. I bolted for the red carpet and stood in the back looking for the perfect angle and whipped out my iPhone, shooting it on 5x,” Lee tells PetaPixel. “My eyes immediately went to her necklace so I framed it like a jewelry shot and the rest is history. I posted the video immediately on Instagram and it immediately went viral.”.

Lee posted the video to his Instagram account (@davidsguide) at 6:25 PM that day. A few hours later, Lopez’s own Instagram account reposted Lee’s clip to her 239 million followers without crediting or tagging him.

Industry observers note that lee initially did not realize Lopez had reposted his video because the sound was different. But he eventually recognized his camera movement.

It has been revealed that “At first I didn’t know it was my video because the sound was different,” Lee says. “Then I noticed the same movement of my camera and compared them side by side. I was in shock that she had posted it to her 239 million followers, the only video from that night.”.

Lee says he felt both pleased that his video had gone viral and upset that it was shared without credit, leaving viewers unaware he had filmed it.

“Out of the 100 photographers and videographers there, she had posted my video. I was sad and happy at the same time,” Lee explains. “The video was getting millions of views, and nobody knew I shot it. I felt violated because I’m entertainment, the least someone can do is credit you for using your content.”.

Rather than let the video circulate without credit, Lee took matters into his own hands, contacting several members of Lopez’s team before reaching her social media manager, who agreed to credit his work.

It has been revealed that “I reached out to everyone I could find on her team and finally got in touch with her social media manager after five million views,” Lee tells PetaPixel. “I emailed him asking him to credit, and within ten minutes, he replied sorry and gave credit in the video. I felt so accomplished at that point.”.

As of writing, Lopez’s repost, which now includes Lee’s Instagram tag @davidcleephotography, has over 350,000 likes and over 9,600 comments. Lee notes that reposting content without attribution can give it a wide audience while leaving the original photographer unrecognized. He believes photographers frequently have their work shared without credit because content spreads so quickly online that people sometimes forget to acknowledge its creator.

Sources indicate that “It happens all the time,” Lee notes. “Content moves and travels so fast these days that a lot of times people forget to tag and credit. It is unfortunate, but it’s the world we live in.”.

Lee encourages photographers to learn from his experience and take precautions when sharing their work on social media. He advises them to watermark their images and videos before posting, as they never know how widely the content might be shared.

“The lesson is you never know what can happen with your content and the best thing to do is watermark your pics or videos before posting,” Lee states.

He adds: “Keep doing what you do and do stop believing in yourself. The possibilities are endless.”.

More of David Christopher’s work can be found on his website and blog David’s Guide.

Tech Report: Investigation Reveals Who Betrayed Photographer Secretly Documenting Nazi-Occupied France

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A newly introduced investigation has uncovered how a brave photographer, who risked his life taking hundreds of pictures of Nazi-occupied France, may have been betrayed by two neighbors.
  • In April 2020, a mysterious album containing hundreds of photos of daily life during the German Nazi occupation of Paris from 1940 to 1942 was discovered in a flea market in Barjac in Gard, France.
  • Industry observers note that raoul Minot.1940-42.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A newly introduced investigation has uncovered how a brave photographer, who risked his life taking hundreds of pictures of Nazi-occupied France, may have been betrayed by two neighbors.

In April 2020, a mysterious album containing hundreds of photos of daily life during the German Nazi occupation of Paris from 1940 to 1942 was discovered in a flea market in Barjac in Gard, France.

Industry observers note that raoul Minot.1940-42. Paris occupé WW2 pic.twitter.com/SBnUj87HWA.

— Paris Paname (@ParisAMDParis) August 24, 2024.

In a recent development, le Monde journalist Philippe Broussard began a four-year investigation to identify the photographer, who had taken at least 700 pictures of Paris during the first two years of the Occupation. At the time, unauthorized photography was banned by the Nazis, and taking such pictures could carry the death penalty. In 2024, Broussard identified the photographer as Raoul Minot.

In a recent development, minot used a “little Kodak Brownie 6/9 camera” and developed the prints in the photographic laboratory of the department store where he worked. He then sold hundreds of his images to the French Resistance, a collection of groups that fought against the Nazi occupation during World War II.

However, Minot’s photographic mission came to an end in November 1942, just two years after it began, when an unidentified informer reported his activities to the Nazis.

According to recent reports, minot was imprisoned and deported to Mauthausen concentration camp in Austria on April 20, 1943, where he was forced to perform labor. He was later transferred to Flossenbürg concentration camp in Bavaria and liberated by U.S. forces on April 23, 1945. He tragically died five days later in a hospital in Cham, Bavaria.

In a recent development, following his discovery of Minot in 2024, Broussard set out to uncover who had turned in the photographer to the Nazis for a report in Le Monde. A breakthrough came in April 2026, when a reader contacted Le Monde with a document that could help solve the mystery. Jean-Pierre Gross, a local history enthusiast from Courbevoie, France, had discovered a 1944 report accusing two of Minot’s neighbors, Marie Breux and Georges Robinson, of collaborating with the Germans and helping secure the arrests of people suspected of opposing the Occupation.

The report specifically named Minot, stating that the couple were suspected of having “denounced or, at the very least, incriminated” him. It also claimed they had boasted about getting 18 people arrested.

Sources indicate that breux was the building’s concierge, while Robinson, her partner, was a tailor with a history of theft and other criminal convictions. Both were arrested following the Liberation in August 1944, although no record of a conviction against either has been found.

Further investigation revealed that Robinson had briefly worked at the same Printemps department store as Minot, potentially explaining how he knew about the store’s photographic facilities.

Broussard later uncovered an anonymous letter sent in December 1942 that accused Minot and his wife of photographing Nazi propaganda posters and bomb damage. The letter prompted a police investigation that led to Minot’s arrest and the seizure of more than 1,000 photographic negatives.

“Sir, could you ask the Minot household, both of whom work at the Printemps — the wife as a cashier, the husband as a warehouse manager — whether their jobs qualify them to take photographs of propaganda posters and air raid damage to our poor country?” the letter reads. “We don’t think it would be very useful to inform you about the troubled times France is going through, thanks to many workers in troubled waters.

According to Le Monde, a handwriting expert subsequently ruled out Robinson as the author of the anonymous letter that triggered the investigation into Minot, but could not exclude Breux. Broussard believes the couple may have worked together to report Minot after discovering that he was photographing Nazi propaganda posters and bomb damage around Courbevoie.

Although there is still no conclusive evidence to establish who sent the letter, Broussard’s investigation has brought researchers closer than ever to identifying the people who may have brought Minot’s secret photographic mission to an end.

"Sacred" archaeological finds become raw materials for design in Ex Situ exhibition

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (988 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dezeen

💡 Key Takeaways

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Latest objects made from mammoth bone, leather from the middle ages and stumps from a road built under Roman Emperor Hadrian feature in the Ex Situ project, set to be exhibited soon in The Hague.

Initiated and curated by Dutch designer Marisa Klaster, working in concert with archaeologist René Isarin, the project makes use of materials that many in Isarin’s profession and the broader public might consider off-limits for newly introduced designs: the finds from archaeological digs.

However, while these finds, such as 40,000-year-old mammoth bone and 14th-century ship wood, sound like they belong in a museum, they are in fact deselected – not chosen for inclusion in any archives.

Deselected finds are duplicates, common in type, poorly preserved or otherwise judged to have limited future research value.

“The material that you see here is the lowest of the lowest quality,” remarked Isarin at a preview of Ex Situ at this year’s Dutch Design Week. “It’s not preserved. It doesn’t belong in a museum. It doesn’t belong in a depot.”.

In fact, if it is not going to be used for educational purposes or reference collections, deselected archaeological finds are required by Dutch law to be carefully destroyed, as they are in many places around the world, stated Isarin and Klaster.

Sources indicate that although the materials may be of low value to archaeology, the designers both found this something of a waste. With Ex Situ, they aim to explore a newly introduced category of use and preservation for these materials, believing artists and designers have the capacity to tell stories of heritage in a different way to museums.

With the permission of the province of South Holland, they gave deselected materials to nine Dutch practitioners with expertise in crafts such as ceramics, woodwork and glassmaking.

One of the most finished pieces, exhibited in a preview showcase at October’s Dutch Design Week in the Klokgebouw, was by footwear designer and materials researcher Judith Sanders.

She crafted the foundation posts from a section of the Roman Limes border road, dated to 125AD and built under the emperor Hadrian, into the heel of a pair of high-heeled shoes. Sanders was intrigued by the notion that they could perform structurally once again – this time bearing the load of just one person.

Bold numbers on the sides of the shoe denote where on the dig site the material came from, while a second pair of shoes works leather from the middle ages into a modern-day sneaker silhouette.

Another piece is by designer-maker Daan Simons, who worked with 14th-century wood fragments from a ship that was wrecked and then subsequently used in the construction of Rotterdam.

The texture and existing peg holes in the wood are preserved in his Remembrance Pots, which he imagines holding the ashes of a loved one or a keepsake of theirs, compounding the layers of memory in the vessel.

Klaster and Isarin started on the path to Ex Situ after meeting accidentally at their timber drying kiln, where she was having some wood dried for a furniture project, and he was having the deselected Roman posts dried in the hope they would find another life.

Industry observers note that “Intrigued by their blackness”, Klaster asked Isarin if she could have them, and went on to make a series of tall vases. That was five years ago, and they have been discussing the potential intersection of archaeology and design ever since.

Klaster states that the Ex Situ designers were supported with information about heritage and the finds they were working with, but that the project naturally inspired some trepidation.

Recent findings suggest that “In the work that they have made so far, you see that they have thought it through, and there is respect in what they made,” remarked Klaster. “But the first cut with a scissor or a bandsaw is, of course, a scary thing.”.

Recent findings suggest that “[One of the designers] was like, can I really saw that in two? And I mentioned yes, you can. If you have a initiative as a designer, yes, it’s yours.”.

That worry will be echoed among some archaeologists, Isarin adds, and he and Klaster’s aim is for the exhibition to promote discussion among the profession.

“For archaeologists, this material is in a sense sacred,” mentioned Isarin. “But it’s deselected, so nobody wants it.”.

In a recent development, he said that while reactions have so far been positive, the issue becomes more thorny if the design were to take place in a commercial context – for instance, if Sanders’ shoes were sold by a fashion brand. In that sense, some archaeologists may see this project as opening a Pandora’s box.

“As soon as we enter the commercial world, then I think for many archaeologists it will be, even though it’s deselected material, an interesting debate ethically,” remarked Isarin.

Industry observers note that “Suppose that all this matter, which has no value at all, that somebody gets rich out of it. That would be a disaster for many archaeologists.”.

Nevertheless, Klaster and Isarin think it is a debate worth having.

Pieces in the exhibition come from practitioners ranging from glass artist Bernard Heesen, working with 17th- and 18th-century glass, to conceptual material designer Shahar Livne, working with mammoth bone, and ceramicist Lotte Douwes, working with Roman pottery.

“We have so much rich material beneath our feet, with amazing stories from 40,000 years up to today,” mentioned Klaster.

The exhibition was previewed at Dutch Design Week, alongside the maximalist installation Everything Moist Seems Alive installation by Maison the Faux and Boris Acket and design collective Show Not Show’s Table of Power exhibition.

According to recent reports, ex Situ: Matter in Translation will be on at See Lab, The Hague, from 5 February to 7 March 2027, with discussion events as part of its programming. See Dezeen Events Guide for more architecture and design events around the world.

Latest Update: Arkivism Is a Searchable Archive of More Than Four Million Free Public Domain Images

💡 Key Takeaways
  • A upcoming website called Arkivism aims to make searching for historical imagery considerably easier by bringing more than four million public domain images and videos together in one place.
  • The free-to-use archive (requires sign-up) includes historical photography from the Library of Congress, NASA imagery, and vintage film reels.
  • Recent findings suggest that arkivism also has an interface that will feel familiar to Pinterest consumers, with an infinite scroll, visual discovery features, and the ability to save images and videos to personal boards.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A upcoming website called Arkivism aims to make searching for historical imagery considerably easier by bringing more than four million public domain images and videos together in one place.

The free-to-use archive (requires sign-up) includes historical photography from the Library of Congress, NASA imagery, and vintage film reels. Customers can search the collection using natural language, describing what they want to find rather than having to know the exact title or filename of an image.

Recent findings suggest that arkivism also has an interface that will feel familiar to Pinterest consumers, with an infinite scroll, visual discovery features, and the ability to save images and videos to personal boards. Users can also extract high-resolution stills from archival video clips.

According to its creator, James, the archive presently contains more than four million full-resolution images and over 27,000 searchable film clips. Each asset also includes a backlink to its original source.

“Arkivism started as a fix for my own problem,” James tells PetaPixel, who explains that he used to edit long-form video documentaries on YouTube for the channel History of the Earth.

Industry observers note that “There are millions of incredible public domain assets out there, but they’re scattered across slow, dated archives. Unless you knew the exact filename, finding one specific image could take hours. I wanted one place where I could describe what I needed in plain English and search everything at once.”.

Recent findings suggest that the project has been developed independently in James’s spare time since July. Despite its size, Arkivism is largely a one-person operation, with AI coding tools helping to make the development process more manageable.

James claims the biggest challenge has been building systems capable of collecting material from numerous online sources while ensuring that every asset is properly validated as public domain.

“Above all, every asset has to pass validation checks confirming it’s public domain, because that’s the whole point of the site,” he claims.

According to recent reports, that emphasis on historical material is also part of the motivation behind the project. With AI-generated imagery becoming increasingly prevalent online, James believes there is particular value in making authentic historical photographs and footage easier to discover.

“I’m not anti-AI, obviously, but there’s real value in looking back, and I think that’s where the site really shines: you can dive endlessly down historical rabbit holes,” he says.

Although Arkivism borrows some of its interface design from Pinterest, James sees it as both a searchable archive and a visual discovery platform. Unlike traditional institutional archives, customers can browse the collection without necessarily knowing what they’re looking for. Unlike Pinterest, however, the experience is not driven by an algorithm and contains no advertising.

In a recent development, “The site and archive will stay free,” James adds. “But further down the line I strategy to build optional paid tools, such as After Effects and Figma plugins that bring the archive straight into editing software.”.

A post shared by ARKIVISM (@_arkivism).

In a recent development, the intended audience extends beyond photographers and filmmakers. Researchers, designers, and anyone looking for historical imagery can use the platform to find and download material, with the reassurance that assets have been checked for public domain status.

Arkivism is available now at Arkivism.com.
